items.title: David Thrussell interview: ‘The deeper I dig, the more I realise the less I know’
items.summary: David Thrussell discusses Snog, Black Lung and the ritual LP "The Reign Of Dead Matter" ahead of Fourscher Festival shows in Erfurt on November 7-8.
items.fullText:
David Thrussell has spent more than three decades using electronic music as something far more than entertainment. With Snog, songs, hooks and dancefloor structures have carried satire and observations about consumerism, obedience, power and mediated reality; Black Lung has provided a darker, harder and more abstract space for exploring technology, control, ritual and systems operating beneath the visible surface. His work with Soma, spoken word and more recent ritual recordings has extended those questions into increasingly different forms.

2026 makes those parallel strands particularly visible. Thrussell released the ritual work “The Reign Of Dead Matter” under his own name, recorded live at the Melbourne Lodge of the Theosophical Society, and joined Darrin Verhagen of Shinjuku Thief for “The Call Of Cthulhu”, a spoken-word and sound-design interpretation of H.P. Lovecraft. A new Black Lung album, “Ordo Ab Chao”, is also imminent, having been recorded live in Paris as a commissioned Masonic soundscape.

European audiences will also have a rare opportunity to see both principal sides of Thrussell’s work almost consecutively. Snog and Black Lung confirmed their only European shows of 2026 at Fourscher Festival in Erfurt: Snog perform on Saturday, November 7, while Black Lung appear on Sunday, November 8.

In this conversation with Side-Line, Thrussell discusses why he increasingly distrusts digital technology, whether subversion can still survive once everything becomes content, the different functions of Snog and Black Lung, ritual as something music can perform rather than merely represent, and why his search for answers has only made the questions larger.

David Thrussell interview

Side-Line: This year you have released work under your own name, collaborated with Shinjuku Thief on “The Call Of Cthulhu”, and are now preparing a new Black Lung album, “Ordo Ab Chao”. These projects are very different in form, but they all seem concerned with systems that are larger than the individual, whether ritual, myth, technology or hidden structures. Do you see them as separate investigations, or are they all circling the same question from different directions?

David Thrussell: Vast cosmic currents surround us and course through us. The so-called ‘occult’ is everywhere and nowhere. Indeed, it is so omniscient that we simply cannot see it. Like asking a fish to describe water, we are often unable to cognate that which animates, directs and controls us. Perhaps, one clear clue is the unified ‘voice’ of the anti-human media and political structure, they incessantly bellow, as a mandatory dogma, that life itself is an aberration, an accident, meaningless and purely material, so you can be sure that all of these statements are the opposite of true. “If you want to make God laugh, tell Him your plans.” Personally, I don’t have a plan. The decision to pursue a project arrives from a combination of instinct, synchronicity and fate. If the winds of inspiration, concepts and personalities coalesce, so be it. It is true, I’m still trying to ask the right questions. The how? and the why? of when and where we are.

Side-Line: With Snog, you spent years examining consumerism, obedience, spectacle and the absurdities of modern power through songs that were often catchy enough to enter the very systems they criticised. In 2026, when critique itself is immediately turned into content, branding and engagement, has satire become harder to make genuinely disruptive?

David Thrussell: Indeed, there is now so much noise, so much competition for fleeting attentions, that it seems counterintuitive, disingenuous (or even immoral) to attempt to even enter the zone. You appear to be correct; subversion has now largely become labelled as another consumer product. Perhaps the sanest approach will be to simply walk away from the whole mad machine or at least deny it the power and dignity of your engagement. As a closet Luddite, I have a deep and instinctual suspicion of technology and the extraordinary power it appears to have (or represent). Indeed, I have proposed a theory that digital technology behaves or manifests as a life form, it seeks dominion, resources and territory just like any other life form. Parasitic organisms are not uncommon in nature, and it would be logical to suggest that digital technologies have been engaged in a symbiotic relationship with humankind. Just as we observe in the natural world, parasitic life forms often kill the host or abandon it when it is no longer useful. Just saying.

Side-Line: Snog’s strength has always been that the songs can function on two levels at once: as music people can physically enjoy, and as texts that may become increasingly uncomfortable once you actually listen to what is being said. Do you still believe the dancefloor can be a political or intellectual space, or has that idea changed for you over time?

David Thrussell: I think I still believe it is theoretically possible. Of course, there are multiple competing narratives at any given time. On the surface, our society appears to be in a race to the bottom. I have often proposed that ‘Idiocracy’ is one of my favourite documentaries. But there are also many other possibilities. How it eventually plays out, I can’t really predict. Humanity has many strengths and many weaknesses. Nature seeks an equilibrium. But my instinct tells me that we are in an undeclared war against non-human forces.

Side-Line: There has not been a new full Snog album since “Eight Offerings For The Undead”, while your recent creative energy has moved strongly through Black Lung, spoken-word work and ritual material. Is Snog currently waiting for the right subject, or has the project itself become something you now approach differently?

David Thrussell: Snog has always been focussed on songs and songwriting. When the songs manifest from the aether, we make a new record, circumstances permitting. I can’t see an advantage in forcing the issue. Right now, gnosis appears to desire to remain unspoken.

Side-Line: The title “Ordo Ab Chao” immediately introduces the old tension between order and chaos. Black Lung has often seemed to work precisely in that unstable zone, where structure is present but never completely secure. On this record, are you more interested in imposing order on chaos, or in discovering that what we call order may simply be one temporary arrangement of it?

David Thrussell: Yes, Black Lung often teeters on the brink of structure and chaos (or noise). The new Black Lung album “Ordo Ab Chao” acknowledges this tension and seeks to channel it into dialogue or even understanding. Recorded live in private concert June 21, 2026, at the Temple des 33, Paris, France, “Ordo Ab Chao” presents a Masonic perspective and indeed was commissioned as a Masonic soundscape to celebrate this fundamental and universal tension. While the world appears to be in steep and irreversible descent into chaos, there are forces just outside your vision that direct, manifest and profit from this era of apparent confusion.

Side-Line: Black Lung and Snog are often described as two different sides of your work, one more song-based and satirical, the other harder, darker and more abstract. But after so many years, do those boundaries still help you creatively, or do the projects increasingly contaminate one another?

David Thrussell: Just as people are (or at least were) unique expressions of a universal consciousness, so Snog and Black Lung are simply different expressions of the same underlying concepts, instincts and provocations.

Side-Line: “The Reign Of Dead Matter” was recorded live at midnight at the Melbourne Lodge of the Theosophical Society and described as ritual music, not simply music inspired by ritual. That distinction is fascinating. What changes when sound is no longer meant to represent an idea or emotion, but is intended to actually do something, to alter attention, space or consciousness?

David Thrussell: The LP “The Reign Of Dead Matter” was implicitly designed to function as the antithesis of popular music. Popular music is a spell cast by a vast and malevolent machine. Its purpose is to enslave, bewitch, benumb and distract. To create legions of soulless androids beholden to an occult project. It has been remarkably successful. “The Reign Of Dead Matter” has the very opposite intent, to action an acknowledgement of the dead, materialistic adversary and ennoble the struggle against the dark, dead void.

Side-Line: There is a recurring tension in your recent work between extremely old structures of meaning, myth, ritual, occult systems, Lovecraft, and very contemporary anxieties around technology, atomisation and information overload. Do you think older myths survive because human fears remain fundamentally the same, or because modernity keeps inventing new machinery for very ancient anxieties?

David Thrussell: Humankind has been robbed of our past. The history of humankind, our world and our place in it has been deliberately obscured, forged and forgotten. Traumatised by a repeating cycle of cataclysm, we are trapped in a holographic shopping mall/Hell created by arch puppeteers and secret societies, like lost children wandering through a ghostly, abandoned amusement park. Howard Phillips Lovecraft may have at times denied a spiritual outlook, but intuitively he understood the false phantasm that masquerades as human ‘society’ with its empty rituals of consumption and obedience. And the deep, dark past that lurks just beyond the glitz and banality of the mall/cathedral. We are indeed children, innocents who guilelessly frolic like carefree ‘Eloi’ as the shadowy ‘Morlocks’ plot and scheme just beneath our feet, just out of our vision. We are the instruments of our own doom, though we rarely glimpse it.

Side-Line: With “The Call Of Cthulhu”, the voice becomes almost architectural. It is not merely carrying text; it determines scale, pacing and psychological pressure. After working so extensively with spoken language rather than conventional song, has that changed the way you think about the human voice inside Snog or Black Lung?

David Thrussell: No doubt it is a cliche to describe the voice as just another instrument. Perhaps it is more constructive to describe the human voice as an “ultra-instrument,” part of the sonic landscape of course, but also capable (in theory, at least) of another layer of cultural messaging, text, literature, history and meaning. Some of the problem arises because the human voice, like almost everything, has become commodified, stripped of meaning and rendered into an artefact of “entertainment”, that most hollow of cultural objects. A battle rages, as we witness the struggle for human connection and meaning inside music, art and literature, so that signifies the deeper conflict between life and the silicon realm.

Side-Line: You have spent decades writing about systems of control, manipulation, consumption and mediated reality. Is there any idea you held twenty or thirty years ago that you now think you got fundamentally wrong, or at least underestimated? I’m interested less in whether the world confirmed your earlier work than in where experience has forced you to revise yourself.

David Thrussell: Indeed, I once fell to the common misapprehension that it was “all about the money”, now I look deeper and see that corporations, materialism and the black magic of the “money system” are merely superficial manifestations of a deeper, more Lovecraftian, more ancient malaise. A conflict that we are largely unconscious of, but are, in fact, surrounded by.

Side-Line: Snog and Black Lung will both appear at Fourscher Festival, on different days, in what are billed as their only European shows of 2026. That creates an unusual situation where an audience can encounter two very different musical identities from the same person almost side by side. Do you want those performances to underline the distance between Snog and Black Lung, or might the festival reveal how much they actually belong to the same internal world?

David Thrussell: Snog and Black Lung are very different manifestations of the same questions. Snog are like the valiant orchestra on the deck of the Titanic, as the ship goes down, we are here to enlighten, elucidate and educate but also to present nursery rhymes and hymns, fables and absurdist comedic relief. A Weimar Cabaret act that chronicles the last moments of the good ship as it plunges under the occult waves. Black Lung creates something different, the soundtrack to the mass ritual that we live every day, the grind of the hungry machine, the delirious demon that wraps its fetid tendrils around our minds and spirits. Summoning demons in order to cast demons out. As it always was and always will be.

Side-Line: After more than three decades of making work that often questions systems, ideologies and the stories people use to organise reality, what still surprises you enough to make you want to create? Has the role of art for you become more about exposing structures, escaping them, or constructing temporary spaces where different ways of thinking are possible?

David Thrussell: The deeper I dig, the more I realise the less I know, the hungrier I get. For knowledge, for understanding, for truth. Just a glimpse. It is the best we can hope for, in a universe built and meant to be beyond our comprehension. As it should be.

About David Thrussell

David Thrussell is an Australian musician, composer and vocalist, active since 1988, whose work spans industrial, EBM, dark ambient, IDM and techno. He formed Snog in Melbourne in 1989 with Tim McGrath and Julia Bourke; Pieter Bourke joined soon after the band’s 1992 debut album “Lies Inc.”, the same year as the single “Corporate Slave”. Snog went on to release “Dear Valued Customer” (1994), “Buy Me… I’ll Change Your Life” (1997), “Third Mall from the Sun” (1999), “Beyond the Valley of the Proles” (2003), “Snog vs. The Faecal Juggernaut of Mass Culture” (2006), “The Last Days of Rome” (2007), “Last of the Great Romantics” (2010), “Babes in Consumerland” (2013), “Compliance” (2015), “Lullabies for the Lithium Age” (2020) and “Eight Offerings for the Undead” (2022), through labels including Machinery Records, Metropolis Records, Zoth Ommog, Shock Records, Hymen Records, Karmic Hit and Psy-Harmonics.

Thrussell launched Black Lung as a more experimental and techno-oriented outlet, debuting with “Silent Weapons for Quiet Wars” in 1994 and continuing through “The Disinformation Plague” (1996), “The Great Architect” (1999), “The Grand Chessboard” (2004), “The Coming Dark Age” (2005), “Full Spectrum Dominance” (2009) and “The Great Manipulator” (2019, Metropolis Records); the project has released almost exclusively through Germany’s Ant-Zen since 1999. Side-Line spoke with Black Lung about technology, governance and the future in June 2024, around the release of the ‘Armageddon’ video and the ‘Euthanasia’ video from the “Depopulate” single. In July 2026, Black Lung and Xavier Morel reworked “Babel” on Psy-Harmonics. Thrussell has also recorded as Soma with Pieter Bourke, releasing “The Inner Cinema” through Ant-Zen in January 2026.

His solo work includes the soundtrack for “The Hard Word” (2002), nominated for Best Original Soundtrack at the 2002 ARIA Music Awards, and the vinyl release “Eros Maximus” (2025). In 2026, Thrussell released the ritual LP “The Reign Of Dead Matter” through Ant-Zen, recorded live at midnight at the Melbourne Lodge of the Theosophical Society, and joined Darrin Verhagen of Shinjuku Thief for “The Call Of Cthulhu”, released through Metropolis Records.

The forthcoming Black Lung album “Ordo Ab Chao”, recorded live at Temple des 33 in Paris on June 21, 2026, as a commissioned Masonic soundscape, precedes Snog and Black Lung’s only confirmed European shows of 2026, at Fourscher Festival in Erfurt, Germany, on November 7 and 8.

items.fullText:
Virgin Birth have released an official video for “The Dead End,” the title track from their six-song EP of the same name, out now via Never Nervous Records. The Louisville, Kentucky industrial punk trio announced the EP in early October, and the full release arrived on streaming platforms on 16 October 2026.

Never Nervous Records describes “The Dead End” as a collection of songs about exhaustion, isolation and dread, continuing the band’s focus on “the darker corners of electronic music, punk, and the increasingly strange world we all find ourselves living in.” Where the band’s earlier releases looked outward at collapse on a larger scale, the label says these six songs feel closer to the ground: more immediate, claustrophobic and personal.

Virgin Birth is Phillip Olympia (vocals, synthesizers, drum machines), Jake Miller (guitars, synth) and Matt Haas (bass). The tracklist runs “The Dead End,” “Pick Up Your Skin,” “Beef Pony,” “Good Book,” “Performative Losing” and “Mystery Man.”

About Virgin Birth

Virgin Birth formed in Louisville, Kentucky, as an industrial synth punk project led by Phillip Olympia and Jake Miller, later joined by bassist Matt Haas. The band released its debut EP, “The Forest,” on 26 May 2023 through Never Nervous Records, followed by the three-song “From Behind” on 14 April 2024, both recorded at The Slaughtered Lamb Studio in Louisville. Virgin Birth released “I Can’t Read” as a single in March 2025 ahead of its debut full-length album, “Total Annihilation,” issued 2 May 2025. “The Dead End” follows that album as the band’s fourth release through Never Nervous Records, with the title track’s video marking the EP’s full arrival on streaming platforms.

items.title: Mesh release video single ‘Fallen Angel’ ahead of November mini-album
items.summary: Mesh release an official video for "Fallen Angel," the title track from their mini-album of the same name, due 27 November on Dependent Records.
items.fullText:
Mesh have released an official video for “Fallen Angel”, the uptempo title track from their upcoming mini-album of the same name, due 27 November 2026 on Dependent Records. The British duo of Mark Hockings and Richard Silverthorn describe the nine-track mini-album as an addendum to this year’s album “The Truth Doesn’t Matter,” built from songs written during that album’s touring cycle.

Richard Silverthorn traces the song back to an earlier working title: “The track, ‘Fallen Angel,’ was born out of a piece of music with the working title ‘Pivot.'” “Mark came up with an inspired lyric and the finished song stood out as more than just a B-side. Enjoy!”

The video follows the release plan Mesh laid out when the mini-album’s tracklist was revealed in September: pre-orders opened 24 September alongside the fourth single from “The Truth Doesn’t Matter,” “Trying to Save You,” and the “Fallen Angel” title track itself arrived as a single on 21 October with this video, ahead of the full CD and vinyl release next month.

The mini-album combines four newly written songs (“Fallen Angel,” “Protect Your Neck,” “Not This Time” and “The Meeting of the Broken”) with the first physical release of “Tilt,” two versions of “Trying to Save You,” a live recording of “The Truth Doesn’t Matter,” and an extended version of “Fallen Angel” itself. Hockings and Silverthorn wrote, recorded and produced the record with Vaughn George on live keyboards and Sean Suleman on live drums, at Mesh HQ and The Summerhouse in Bristol, and mixed by Olaf Wollschläger and Mesh at Cottonbeat Studio in Burscheid, Germany. “Fallen Angel” is set for release as a jewel-case CD, a clear vinyl LP limited to 500 copies, and a standard black vinyl LP.

About Mesh

Mesh are a British electronic band from Bristol, formed in 1991 when singer Mark Hockings and keyboard player Richard Silverthorn met at a concert. Silverthorn’s former bandmate Neil Taylor soon joined on keyboards. Signed to the Swedish label Memento Materia, the trio released the EP “Fragile” in 1994, followed by the album “In This Place Forever” in 1996 and the breakthrough “The Point At Which It Falls Apart” in 1999. Sony Records picked the band up for 2002’s “Who Watches Over Me,” and 2006’s “We Collide” was produced by former Depeche Mode producer Gareth Jones.

Taylor left in 2006 and Hockings and Silverthorn continued as a duo with an augmented live line-up, signing to Dependent Records for Europe and Metropolis Records for the Americas. German producer Olaf Wollschläger, who produced 2009’s “A Perfect Solution,” has worked with the band on every record since. “Automation Baby” (2013) topped the European Alternative Charts, and “Looking Skyward” (2016) reached number 12 in Germany. Mesh announced “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” with the single “Exile” in January 2026, followed by “Hey Stranger” in February and “This World” in March, then toured behind the album through the spring. “Fallen Angel,” built from songs Hockings and Silverthorn wrote during that touring cycle, now carries the story into a mini-album of its own.

items.title: “I Slipped Right Under That Fence” — A Dog Makes Its Getaway in Post-Punk Outfit SMILE’s Video for “Gotta Run”
items.summary: Faster than it takes for hair to dry Faster than the other dogs, tearing down wet clothes Leaving a city can be a straightforward matter of roads, tolls, gas, and… The post “I Slipped Right Under That Fence” — A Dog Makes Its Getaway in Post-Punk Outfit SMILE’
items.fullText:
Faster than it takes for hair to dry
Faster than the other dogs, tearing down wet clothes

Leaving a city can be a straightforward matter of roads, tolls, gas, and mileage; escaping a family that confuses love with obedience can be considerably messier. Cruelty acquires the respectable name of discipline, old wounds get passed off as birthmarks, and the people who bite hardest still expect you to come when called. Eventually, survival requires finding a gap beneath the fence, with the rest of the pack still tearing into one another behind you.

Based between Amsterdam, Berlin, and Cologne, post-punk quintet SMILE explores that vicious family logic on “Gotta Run,” a new single introducing their forthcoming second album, Gun-Shy, due January 22, 2027, via Vienna’s Siluh Records.

A deep drumbeat and a thick, dirty bassline drive the song forward, with the guitar sawing beneath a rhythm section that fills most of the available floor space. Rubee Fegan’s abrasive, near-spoken delivery recalls Kim Gordon’s work with Sonic Youth, rising to shouts as the pressure builds. The arrangement carries the unruly physicality of late-’80s and early-’90s alternative rock, giving its agitation plenty of room to move. Later, gentle guitar strumming opens space around the voice, the rhythm eases, and Fegan lowers her volume as the song gradually slows to a halt.

The lyrics render escape as a bodily ordeal: exposed skin, chafed thighs, the raw friction of getting away. Kinship offers scant protection in a yard where littermates bite until they scar, then wave the damage away as a birthmark. Choosing a switch lends punishment the grotesque sheen of consent, while the shift from “You wouldn’t recognize if they came back” to “You wouldn’t recognize if I came back” turns estrangement inward. The scrawny runt slips beneath the fence as the others rage in the yard. To be “not quite homesick yet” feels like a welcome reprieve from the pack.

Created by Rubee Fegan, Taylor Cappage, and Olivia Martinez, the accompanying video carries that restlessness through Albuquerque, New Mexico, Fegan’s hometown. Dressed as a pink poodle, she walks and drives through a city caught in handheld fragments: power lines, passing cars, scrap heaps, neighbourhood walls, a black cat, neon signs against the dark. The mountains remain visible beyond the sprawl. Read alongside the lyrics, the costume gives the song’s imagery of training, captivity, and escape an absurdly cheerful public face.

Writing in the album’s press text, Annika Henderson, better known as Anika, offers a suitably breathless account:

“Lead single, ‘Gotta Run’ is an escape room of urgent, punk, claustrophobic, yet upbeat sounds, held in by fast drums. They’ve got a point and won’t stop til you join their side, til you cave in. The accompanying playful video of handy cam street scenes, fishnets and animal heads, place you in a seedy pseudo-reality, more akin to computer game, GTA.

“The goal is to get out.” They tell me. “GTA 6, first person, free world exploration style. It’s about leaving and why; what a violent system teaches the body to do even after escape.”

Broken cars, broken cities, in this gritty existence; Bright lights and dogs drooling; Motorcycles ripping up tarmac; You gotta run but where or why?

The flow breakdown comes early, yet not letting you off the leash for long. Lock jaw, it transforms into a whole different song. Now they play with their food, their catch, or perhaps stop to catch their breath. Gotta run faster than it takes wet hair to dry – become slack now. Taunting you, yet your legs and arms are bound.”

Watch the video for Gotta Run below:

Gun-Shy was recorded with Olaf Opal at Bear Cave studio in Cologne, drawing on demos that include recordings made in Albuquerque. The sessions retained some first takes alongside more deliberately crafted studio elements, carrying the music’s initial impulses into the finished record.

Formed by friends during the pandemic, SMILE is comprised of Rubee True Fegan, Marius Szarnych, Sebastian Lessel, Max Schmidt, and Lars Fritzsche. The new album follows their 2022 debut EP, I Hate It Here, and 2023 debut LP, Price of Progress. Since then, support dates with Fontaines D.C., tours with Touché Amoré, and shows alongside Squid have sharpened the band’s command of dynamics and intensity.

Gun-Shy is out on January 22, 2027, via Vienna’s Siluh Records. Listen to Gotta Run below, and order the single here.

items.fullText:
French/Greek no wave and dark wave duo Sensitive Content has released its debut album, ‘Romantic Asthmatic’, digitally on 2 October 2026. A limited transparent-vinyl edition of 200 copies, including a colour insert, follows on 23 October through the Italian label Manic Depression.

The eight-track album centers on romantic and sexual relationships, moving from the start of a connection to its end. The band describes the record as addressing “the huge factor of the collapsing society that divides humans with animals,” alongside themes of toxic masculinity and power control. Sensitive Content calls “Romantic Asthmatic” an “accurate description of what we experience in our dark dead end times,” with romance and love cast as an escape that fails once a relationship turns destructive.

The tracklist for “Romantic Asthmatic” runs: “Grievious Blow,” “Knifer,” “Gynaika,” “Charisma Phantasma,” “Heatwave,” “Tu Veux Un Sac?,” “They Run” and “To Telos.” The first single, “Grievious Blow,” has an accompanying video.

About Sensitive Content

Sensitive Content is a French/Greek no wave and dark wave duo. “Romantic Asthmatic” is the project’s debut album, released digitally through its own Bandcamp page before the vinyl edition’s release on the Italian label Manic Depression. No further biographical details about the duo have been made public at the time of writing.

Blood&Ink releases “The Pharmacist Pageant,” a track from the industrial glam metalcore project’s debut album “Rusted Soaked Stage Ritual.” The album is self-released and available on Bandcamp, with streaming-store distribution through DistroKid.

Blood&Ink is the solo project of Burlington, New Jersey vocalist and songwriter William Forfar, who also performs as Reck. “Rusted Soaked Stage Ritual” contains three tracks: “Filthy Circuit Baptism,” “The Pharmacist Pageant” and “Machines Learned to Dance.” Forfar wrote and performed all three songs. “The Pharmacist Pageant” addresses medication, trauma and the struggle to hold on to one’s identity. About Blood&Ink

Blood&Ink is the independent industrial glam metalcore project of William Forfar, known on stage as Reck, based in Burlington, New Jersey. The project blends machine-driven heaviness, theatrical atmosphere and a first-person vocal approach built around trauma, identity and survival, under the guiding line “Let the Blood flow through the Ink.”

“Rusted Soaked Stage Ritual,” released 19 October 2026, is Blood&Ink’s debut, self-released through Bandcamp with distribution via DistroKid. The three-track set moves from the “mechanical aggression and defiance” of opener “Filthy Circuit Baptism,” through “The Pharmacist Pageant,” to the closing “Machines Learned to Dance,” which contrasts human feeling with a more mechanical world. items.title: Martin Gore, His Daughter Johnnie Lee, and Cliff Damavandi Commune With the Departed on “Cross Whisper”
items.summary: A bird at the window can become a peculiar kind of correspondent after someone you love has died, its arrival gathering a meaning no sensible explanation can quite dispel. Grief… The post Martin Gore, His Daughter Johnnie Lee, and Cliff Damavandi Commune With
items.fullText:
A bird at the window can become a peculiar kind of correspondent after someone you love has died, its arrival gathering a meaning no sensible explanation can quite dispel. Grief attunes us to such visitations: a sound in the garden, a small creature returning to the same pane of glass, a persistent interruption in an otherwise ordinary afternoon. Suddenly, the world seems to brim with messages, all awaiting translation.

That uncertainty finds its electronic form on Cross Whisper, a new collaboration between Depeche Mode’s Martin Gore and artist and lyricist Cliff Damavandi, with additional vocals from Gore’s daughter Johnnie Lee. Released on October 20 through Mute as MG x CD + JL =, the single gives an intimate encounter with loss a shared musical language.

The piece began during a conversation among friends about unexplained phenomena. Gore remarked that “he wouldn’t be surprised by anything” before recounting a series of encounters with birds around moments of bereavement. One particularly persistent visitor tapped ferociously at his studio window; two days later, he learned that a close friend had died. The experience left him considering the symbolism long attached to birds, and whether these visitors might be harbingers or messengers. Gore recalls:

“I was out with some friends and we started talking about death so I shared that whenever someone close to me has died, birds start appearing, sometimes arriving every day for a year outside my window. When my mother died, a bird came, and again when my dog passed. When my cat died, a bird came into the house and flew downstairs into the room where it slept!”

Damavandi was so moved by the account that he wrote lyrics, which Gore then set to music. Their exchange gives the song a deeply personal foundation: Gore offers a memory, and Damavandi finds language for the feeling it leaves behind. As Damavandi explains:

“When Martin was sharing his story, he was so alive, and I could feel the story as well as hear it. There was an otherness that compelled me to write the words.”

Whispered voices introduce the track before gradually giving way to Gore’s synthesizers. The murmurs return in waves between melodic passages, accompanied by an insistent hammering that mirrors the bird at his studio window. Read against its origins, that repeated knock becomes an unsettling gesture, an everyday sound carrying the weight of an unanswered question. The arrangement gives physical form to the uncertainty in Gore’s story, allowing a remembered disturbance to keep interrupting the present.

The accompanying visualiser was filmed in Japan and England by Luca Bailey. Watch Cross Whisper below:

The release also brings together five remixers: Brazilian techno DJ and producer ANNA; techno artist, DJ, and label head Regis; Dutch techno artist Vera Grace; boothnavy; and British electronic musician Martin Jenkins, working as Pye Corner Audio. Their versions extend the collaboration across a six-track vinyl edition, with a further Regis remix included in the full digital release.

Cross Whisper is available digitally now. A limited transparent green 12-inch, housed in an embossed sleeve, follows through Mute on December 4, 2026. The full digital edition arrives on January 15, 2027, adding Regis’ Cellular Drift Remix to the six tracks featured on the vinyl.

items.title: NYC Post-Punk Outfit London Plane Skewer the Cult of Obedience in Video for “NATION NATION”
items.summary: The regency is strong Black boots match my skeleton mask And my instincts are all gone Now I’m something to fear The most dangerous idiot in any political movement is the one who… The post NYC Post-Punk Outfit London Plane Skewer the Cult of Obedience in Video
items.fullText:
The regency is strong 
Black boots match my skeleton mask
And my instincts are all gone
Now I’m something to fear

The most dangerous idiot in any political movement is the one who has surrendered his ability to think and discovered, with tremendous satisfaction, that obedience provides a wonderful substitute for having a personality. Give him a uniform, a charismatic lunatic to worship, and a few convenient enemies, and suddenly the poor bastard believes himself an instrument of history. Fascism has always depended upon this peculiar species of enthusiastic mediocrity, the ordinary creep who mistakes submission for strength and cruelty for patriotic duty. With NATION NATION, New York City’s six-piece London Plane plunge into the diseased psychology of the true believer, serving up nearly three minutes of manic post-punk absurdity with enough political venom to make a demagogue choke on his own campaign slogans.

Produced by Carlos Dengler, formerly of Interpol, the track hurtles forward on frantic guitars, a muscular rhythmic charge, and feverish vocals that suggest somebody enjoying a spectacular psychological collapse. The hooks are infectious, the momentum almost indecently cheerful, and the whole grotesque enterprise resembles a fascist pep rally conducted by people who have consumed considerably more pharmaceuticals than their doctors would recommend.

“NATION NATION is sung from the perspective of the sycophant, the idiot-turned-weapon,” says frontman David Mosey. “We allowed ourselves to be a bit absurd on this song, and Dengler encouraged and embraced the eccentric, even demented side of the band. The bright, frenetic, blitzkrieg guitars and vocals suggest that our subject is probably high and quite ready to sacrifice himself on behalf of his dear leader. It is a somewhat uncomfortable place to be, but we put ourselves in his jackboots for nearly three minutes every time we perform the song.”

The accompanying video, directed by Zane Rizvi-Riemer and Max Burbey, takes this horrifying little proposition to its logical conclusion. Two ordinary-looking men knock on doors with the bland determination of political canvassers or religious missionaries, their apparent harmlessness gradually giving way to something considerably more sinister. Through Soviet-style expressionist imagery, exaggerated close-ups of leering faces, darting eyes, and hands dispensing pills, the film reveals an authoritarian recruitment operation unfolding beneath the reassuring appearance of everyday civic life. The pharmaceutical imagery recalls the Nazis’ documented use of methamphetamine.

In addition to the nonstop horrors on everyday doomscrolls in the modern era, the video draws upon the dystopian horrors of Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World and George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, combining the chemical pacification and willing surrender of individual thought envisioned by Huxley with Orwell’s machinery of surveillance, ideological conformity, and manufactured enemies, through which ordinary citizens become enthusiastic accomplices in their own subjugation. Between the two dystopias lies the terrifying possibility that fascism requires remarkably little encouragement to spread, particularly when its foot soldiers have been convinced that obedience is a virtue and persecution a public service. Evil, apparently, has learned to smile politely before introducing itself.

Watch below:

NATION NATION appears on London Plane’s forthcoming third album, Villains Heroes Ghosts, expected in early 2027 via Declared Goods. Dengler’s first production work for another artist suggests an intriguing creative partnership, particularly for a band whose international membership has already brought considerable character to New York Howl (2018) and Bright Black (2022).

And in an era when political fanaticism increasingly resembles mass entertainment, London Plane have produced a savage reminder of how easily the jackboot finds another willing foot.

items.title: Lustmord – ‘Trinity’ (Digital – Lustmord)
items.summary: Side-Line review of Lustmord's "Trinity": a 2020 dark ambient album built on Los Alamos and White Sands field recordings of the first atomic test.
items.fullText:
The Architecture of Nuclear Fear. Side-Line contributor Karo Kratochwil reviews “Trinity”, the 2020 dark ambient album by Lustmord. Brian Williams released the six-track digital album independently via Bandcamp on 2 October 2020, built from field recordings made at Los Alamos National Laboratory and the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, the sites tied to the first atomic bomb test. Ant-Zen later issued “Trinity” as a limited CD with a 48-page hardcover book, since sold out at source.

I was born in the early 1980s, close enough to the generation that lived through the Second World War for its memory still to exist inside ordinary family conversation. My grandparents had experienced the war and sometimes spoke about it. Not about Hiroshima or Nagasaki specifically, but about fear, deprivation, uncertainty and the ways in which people adapt to circumstances that should never become normal. The historical distance was already there, but the memory had not yet become entirely abstract.

That is one of the reasons listening to Lustmord’s “Trinity” now feels so unsettling. The album deals with events of 1945, but it does not remain safely contained within history. I do not mean that our present moment is identical to 1939, because historical situations never repeat themselves so neatly, but I cannot entirely escape the parallel. There is something familiar in the accumulation of geopolitical tension, the hardening of political divisions, ongoing wars, competing spheres of influence and the strange ability of everyday life to continue while the language of escalation becomes increasingly ordinary. What unsettles me is less the idea that history is repeating itself than the possibility that people living before earlier catastrophes may also have experienced danger gradually, as something that entered public life in increments until it no longer felt exceptional.

“Trinity” was originally commissioned by Unsound Festival in 2012 and later developed into the album released in 2020. Its six pieces are built partly from recordings made at Los Alamos, where the atomic bomb was developed, and at the New Mexico test site associated with the first nuclear detonation, alongside archival material from Los Alamos National Laboratory. “Twilight: Los Alamos” also incorporates the voice of J. Robert Oppenheimer. These documentary elements matter because the album does not invent an apocalyptic scenario. It works with traces of an event that actually happened.

At 5:30 a.m. on July 16, 1945, the Trinity test demonstrated that nuclear destruction was no longer theoretical. Less than a month later, atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Whatever political and military arguments surround those decisions, the psychological consequence extends far beyond the final weeks of the war. Humanity had acquired the ability to destroy on a scale that radically altered the meaning of technological power, and that knowledge has remained part of political reality ever since.

What makes Lustmord’s treatment of this subject so effective is the refusal of spectacle.

The obvious musical response to an atomic explosion would be excess: enormous crescendos, overwhelming volume, violent percussion, catastrophic distortion. “Trinity” does almost the opposite. The music is sparse, slow and remarkably controlled. Low frequencies move beneath the surface, distant resonances expand gradually, archival voices appear without theatrical staging, and large stretches of the album seem to exist somewhere between sound and silence.

For me, this restraint matters. A more spectacular treatment could easily turn nuclear destruction into aesthetic excitement. The mushroom cloud is already one of the most visually familiar images of the twentieth century, and its scale can become perversely fascinating when removed from the human reality behind it. Lustmord avoids that trap. There are no musical fireworks here, and I think there should not be. In this context, excessive sonic drama could almost feel indecent because it would risk transforming technological horror into entertainment.

Instead, “Trinity” concentrates on the psychological space surrounding the event.

Fear does not always produce screaming. Sometimes it produces stillness. The body freezes, the voice disappears, perception narrows and something too large to process is experienced first as silence. That sensation runs through the album. Its tension rarely feels like panic in motion; it feels closer to the moment in which panic has not yet found a physical outlet.

This is where Lustmord’s understanding of ambient music becomes particularly impressive. Ambient composition at this level does not simply provide atmosphere around a subject. It controls distance, scale, duration and attention. The listener becomes aware of how long a sound persists, how much empty space surrounds it and how little information is actually required to produce unease. The music often works below the level of intellectual analysis. The body reacts first.

“Twilight: Los Alamos” places the listener in the world of preparation, research and knowledge. From there, “Oak Ridge,” “Dusk: White Sands,” “Journey of the Dead Man” and “Surface Zero” gradually move closer to the moment when theoretical possibility became physical fact. The sequencing creates a sense of approach without turning the record into a conventional narrative.

“Dusk: White Sands” is especially effective because the landscape itself seems to carry the tension. There is no need to reproduce the explosion sonically. The title, the location and the historical knowledge already determine how the sound is heard. “Surface Zero” follows the same approach. The dread comes from what the listener knows stands behind the music.

The final piece, “A New Dawn: Hiroshima,” carries perhaps the most difficult emotional weight of the album. The phrase “new dawn” would normally suggest renewal, but here it belongs to a world entering the nuclear age through the destruction of an actual city. The title therefore brings together technological achievement, historical rupture and moral unease without requiring the music to dramatize any of them overtly.

That is where “Trinity” becomes more than an album about the atomic bomb itself. It becomes an album about living after the bomb.

The knowledge cannot be undone. Nuclear weapons exist within political systems, military doctrines and strategic calculations, but psychologically they also exist as a permanent background possibility. Most of the time, that possibility remains outside conscious attention. People work, raise children, travel, argue, fall in love and plan their futures while weapons capable of destroying entire cities remain part of the geopolitical structure around them.

Lustmord’s sparse language suits that condition with remarkable precision. The music does not bombard the listener with horror. It allows the horror to remain latent, present but not constantly visible, which is arguably much closer to the way nuclear threat exists in ordinary life.

This is also why “Trinity” feels particularly relevant now. Not because 2026 is simply another 1939, and not because catastrophe is inevitable, but because the album reminds us how easily technological possibility can outlive the historical circumstances that produced it. The world that created the first atomic bomb is gone, but the knowledge, infrastructure and political logic surrounding nuclear weapons remain.

What Lustmord achieves is therefore less an illustration of the explosion than an exploration of its psychological aftermath. The album holds dread, awe, anticipation and the strange paralysis that can accompany awareness of something too large to comprehend fully. Its power lies in reduction. Every low-frequency vibration, distant voice and stretch of near-silence is allowed to carry weight because nothing around it is unnecessarily enlarged.

For a work concerned with one of the most destructive technologies ever created, “Trinity” is strikingly restrained, and that restraint is precisely what makes it convincing. The album understands that terror does not always arrive with noise. Sometimes it is experienced as the sudden awareness of what human beings are capable of, followed by the much more difficult task of continuing to live with that knowledge.

About Lustmord

Lustmord is the long-running project of Brian Williams, who began working under the name in 1980 after encouragement from Chris Carter and Cosey Fanni Tutti. Over the following decade, field recording, industrial experimentation and collaborations gradually formed the sonic language that culminated in “Heresy” in 1990, an album widely regarded as one of the defining dark ambient works of that era.

Williams’ work has always extended beyond solo albums. He has collaborated with artists including SPK, John Balance, Chris & Cosey, Current 93, Nurse With Wound, Melvins, Tool, Puscifer and Karin Park, while also contributing to more than 40 motion pictures, as well as video games and television. After relocating to Los Angeles in 1993, he increasingly took on soundtrack and sound-design work, with credits connected to films including “The Crow,” “Underworld” and Paul Schrader’s “First Reformed.”

That background is important when approaching “Trinity.” Lustmord’s music has long been less about conventional composition than about constructing environments through scale, resonance, field recordings and carefully controlled low-frequency sound. “Trinity” sits very naturally within that wider body of work, but its historical subject gives those techniques an unusually concrete and disturbing focus, the same catalogue this review now joins.

items.title: In Strict Confidence releases ‘Fever’ single and video
items.summary: In Strict Confidence release new single "Fever" with an official video, out 16 October 2026 via Minuswelt, with remixes by Ash Code and Controlled Fusion.
items.fullText:
German EBM and electro-industrial act In Strict Confidence has released a new single, “Fever“, together with an official music video, on 16 October 2026 via Minuswelt. The band describes the song as a first glimpse into the world of its upcoming album.

The three-track single pairs the original version of “Fever” with two remixes: one by Controlled Fusion, and another by Italian darkwave act Ash Code. “Fever” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp, Spotify and Apple Music.

In Strict Confidence’s ‘Fever’ single

Alongside the digital single, In Strict Confidence has also made eight additional mixes of “Fever” available on its Bandcamp page. In Strict Confidence has upcoming shows confirmed in Austria, Germany and Spain into 2027, including dates in Vienna, Weissenhäuser Strand, Oberhausen and Benidorm.

About In Strict Confidence

In Strict Confidence formed in Germany in 1989 under the name Seal of Secrecy, renaming itself In Strict Confidence in 1992, when the group narrowed from a quartet to the duo of Dennis Ostermann and Jörg Schelte. Stefan Vesper, a member of the original line-up, left in 1992 and returned to the band in 2001. Heidi Pulkkinen, credited as HayDee Sparks, joined on guitars in 2008, and Nina de Lianin joined on vocals and lyrics in 2009, alongside Ostermann and Schelte in the band’s current line-up.

The band released its debut album, “Cryogenix”, in 1996 on Zoth Ommog, followed by “Face the Fear” and “Love Kills!” as it moved toward Metropolis Records and WTII Records for international distribution. Albums “Mistrust the Angels” (2002), “Holy” (2004), “Exile Paradise” (2006), “La Parade Monstrueuse” (2010), “Utopia” (2012), “The Hardest Heart” (2016) and “Hate2Love” (2018) followed, with Side-Line covering the band’s reissue of “La Parade Monstrueuse” as a 3CD set and the release of “The Hardest Heart” in three formats. In 2018, the band issued the “Mercy” EP, later following it with a limited double-vinyl edition. In 2021, the band marked the 25th anniversary of its debut with the “Cryogenix (25 Years Edition)“. In Strict Confidence now returns with “Fever” ahead of a new studio album.

items.title: Martin Gore and Cliff Damavandi release ‘Cross Whisper’ as MG x CD + JL =, with vocals by Gore’s daughter
items.summary: Depeche Mode‘s Martin Gore has released a new electronic single, “Cross Whisper“, in collaboration with...
items.fullText:
Depeche Mode‘s Martin Gore has released a new electronic single, “Cross Whisper“, in collaboration with artist and lyricist Cliff Damavandi and with vocals from Gore’s daughter Johnnie Lee. Credited to the newly formed MG x CD + JL =, the track came out digitally on 20 October 2026 via Mute, with a limited transparent green 12″ vinyl edition following on 4 December.

The song grew out of a conversation about unexplainable phenomena, in which Gore described birds appearing at moments when people and animals close to him died, including an incident in which a bird tapped repeatedly at his studio window two days before he learned a close friend had died. Gore recounted the pattern: “I was out with some friends and we started talking about death so I shared that whenever someone close to me has died, birds start appearing, sometimes arriving every day for a year outside my window. When my mother died, a bird came, and again when my dog passed. When my cat died, a bird came into the house and flew downstairs into the room where it slept!”

Damavandi, who wrote the lyrics that Gore then set to music, described how the story prompted him to write: “When Martin was sharing his story, he was so alive, and I could feel the story as well as hear it. There was an otherness that compelled me to write the words.”

“Cross Whisper” opens with whispered vocals before Gore’s synthesizers enter, with a recurring percussive motif that echoes the bird’s tapping at his studio window.

Gore produced “Cross Whisper” and wrote it with Damavandi. The two share lead vocals and synthesizers, with Arielle Sitrick and Johnny Lee on background vocals. Marta Salogni, who also mixed and engineered Depeche Mode’s “Memento Mori”, handled the mix.

The 12″ single, released via Mute in a limited transparent green edition with an embossed sleeve, pairs the original 5:46 track with five additional remixes. Vinyl orders for the UK and EU go through Mute Bank; Gore’s Bandcamp page ships the 12″ from the US and offers a digital pre-order that delivers the original track immediately.

Mute also released an official visualiser for “Cross Whisper”, filmed in Japan and England by Luca Bailey.

‘Cross Whisper’ remixes on vinyl and digital

Remixes come from ANNA, a Brazilian techno DJ and producer; Regis, a techno artist, DJ and label head; Vera Grace, a Dutch techno artist; Pye Corner Audio, the British hauntologist also known as Martin Jenkins; and boothnavy.

Side A: “Cross Whisper”, “Cross Whisper (Regis’ Learn to See Mix)”, “Cross Whisper (Vera Grace Remix)”
Side B: “Cross Whisper (ANNA Remix)”, “Cross Whisper (Pye Corner Audio Remix)”, “Cross Whisper (boothnavy’s Murmuration Remix)”

The digital release on January 15, 2027 adds a seventh track, “Cross Whisper (Regis’ Cellular Drift Remix)”, which is not part of the vinyl tracklist.

About Martin Gore and Cliff Damavandi

Martin Gore was born in London on July 23, 1961. In 1980 he joined Andrew Fletcher and Vince Clarke in the Basildon, Essex group Composition of Sound, which became Depeche Mode after Dave Gahan joined as lead singer. The band released its debut album “Speak and Spell” on October 5, 1981. After Clarke left later that year, Gore became Depeche Mode’s principal songwriter, alongside keyboards, guitar, backing vocals and occasional lead vocals.

Gore’s work outside the band has also appeared on Mute. “Counterfeit“, an EP of cover versions, came out on June 12, 1989. “Counterfeit²”, with eleven covers of songs that shaped his own writing, followed on April 28, 2003. He reunited with Clarke as VCMG for the instrumental electronic album “Ssss”, released on March 12, 2012. His solo album “MG“, sixteen electronic instrumentals recorded at his Electric Ladyboy studio in Santa Barbara, California, came out on April 27, 2015. The five-track instrumental EP “The Third Chimpanzee”, introduced with the track “Mandrill“, followed on January 29, 2021, and “The Third Chimpanzee Remixed” on August 20, 2021.

Depeche Mode’s Andrew Fletcher died on May 26, 2022, after which the band continued as the duo of Gahan and Gore and released their fifteenth studio album, “Memento Mori“, on March 24, 2023. The concert film “Depeche Mode: M”, shot over three nights in Mexico City during the 2023 tour, premiered at the Tribeca Festival in June 2025 and reached Netflix on January 9, 2026. On March 6, 2026, the band issued “Universal Soldier” on War Child’s charity album “HELP(2)”.

Cliff Damavandi is an artist and lyricist. “Cross Whisper” is his first released work with Gore, and no earlier music releases under his name are listed in public discographies.

In Gore’s solo catalog, “Cross Whisper” is the first new release since “The Third Chimpanzee Remixed” in August 2021, and the first under the MG x CD + JL = name.

items.title: EVA X sets release date for new album ‘TURBOPINK’
items.summary: EVA X announces her second album "TURBOPINK", out 6 November 2026 on CD and digital, with a cover of Korn's "Twisted Transistor".
items.fullText:
US goth-industrial artist Eva X will release her second album, “TURBOPINK“, on 6 November 2026. The nine-track record follows her 2022 debut, “I Dream of a Reality”, and includes a cover of Korn‘s “Twisted Transistor”. It will be available on CD and digital formats worldwide.

“TURBOPINK” is preceded by two already-released singles, “Dopamine Blind” and “Fiction”, and by “Dance in Shadows“, which Side-Line covered on its release on 18 September 2026. Eva X wrote and recorded the album after touring across North America for her debut, during which the project grew from a solo studio act into a four-piece live band.

Eva X’s ‘TURBOPINK’ tracklist and sound

The album mixes industrial, electronica and metal, with elements of J-pop. Its nine tracks are “Love.Hate.Paradise”, “Dopamine Blind”, “Otherside”, “Fiction”, “Cross My Heart”, “I Remember Me”, “Dance in Shadows”, “Mother Mirror” and a cover of Korn’s “Twisted Transistor”. “Dance in Shadows” was written by Eva X collaborator Gaby Gustafson and carries a breakbeat remix by Stoneburner on its single release. “TURBOPINK” is available to pre-order on Bandcamp ahead of its 6 November release on CD and digital formats.

About Eva X

Eva X’s project dates to 2019, when she began posting self-produced tracks that fused synthwave, industrial, power pop and metal, drawing a following in the goth and industrial scene. She released the video “Machine” in 2021, followed by her debut album, “I Dream of a Reality“, on Distortion Productions in 2022, which appeared on several “best of 2022” year-end lists. In 2024, she released the single and video “Dopamine Blind“. She went on to tour North America, performing at New Jersey’s Dark Force Fest, Seattle’s Mechanismus Festival and Calgary’s Terminus, and expanded the project into a four-piece band along the way. In September 2026, she previewed her second album with the single “Dance in Shadows”. Eva X now closes out that album cycle with “TURBOPINK”, due 6 November 2026.

items.title: Felsenreich Find a New Pace on Their Sixth Album “Motiv und Tempo”
items.summary: Felsenreich release their sixth album Motiv und Tempo on Danse Macabre. Wave and post-punk tinged gothic rock produced by Frenzy Erl
items.fullText:
SponsoredFelsenreich

After more than 25 years in Germany’s dark music scene, Felsenreich have released their sixth stu­dio album “Motiv und Tempo” via Danse Macabre. The record entered the Deutsche Alternative Charts (DAC) at num­ber 5 in week 33 and held on at num­ber 7 the fol­low­ing week. It also shows the band tak­ing a notice­ably dif­fer­ent approach.

A Leaner Sound for Felsenreich

The band’s earli­er albums leaned towards the opu­lent. On “Motiv und Tempo” the songs are built in a much more dir­ect way and often recall post-punk and wave. What has not changed is the band’s knack for mem­or­able melod­ies. Wide gui­tars and float­ing key­boards carry them, with a cool and restrained vocal deliv­ery on top. The lyr­ics are partly in German and partly in English.

The album was recor­ded at the Highline Studio in Munich, where Felsenreich were joined by musi­cians from the wave band Escape With Romeo. Their drum­mer Frenzy Erl pro­duced the record, as he has done for Felsenreich since 2017.

Strength Drawn from the Past

One theme runs through the whole album. Looking back at what has been can give you the strength to cope with the present, how­ever hard it may be. This is the motif behind the title, set against the pace of our times. The band them­selves describe the album as a mes­sage of encouragement.

For DJs the band recom­mend “Nightboundtrain” as a start­ing point, along with “I Will Tell You” and “Glorious Solution”. The lyr­ic video for “Über uns der Himmel” is a good first look at the new material.

About Felsenreich

Felsenreich were foun­ded in 1998 by Mathias Sohn, Renato Wesely and Carsten Schaller, who all share vocal duties. Sohn also plays key­boards and trum­pet, Wesely the acous­tic gui­tar and Schaller the elec­tric gui­tar. Their name stands for a self-con­tained music­al realm that is meant to stay sol­id as rock in chan­ging times.

Musically they move between goth­ic rock and post-punk, often with a strong elec­tron­ic side. Since 2008 their albums have appeared on Danse Macabre, the label foun­ded by the late Bruno Kramm of Das Ich.

Felsenreich have shared stages with acts such as Marilyn Manson and Project Pitchfork and have played the Wave-Gotik-Treffen in Leipzig sev­er­al times. In 2010 they added an acous­tic and lit­er­ary pro­gramme, which also took them to Ireland for live shows.

Listen to “Felsenreich – Motiv und Tempo” on Spotify

items.title: Gare Terminus previews ‘Kenosis’ album with ‘Wisdom of the Forest’ video
items.summary: Luxembourg neofolk/noise project Gare Terminus shared the video for "Wisdom of the Forest" ahead of its "Kenosis" album, out 31 October 2026 on Abanbandonment.
items.fullText:
Luxembourg-based neofolk, noise and experimental project Gare Terminus shared a video for “Wisdom of the Forest” on 18 October 2026, taken from its forthcoming album “Kenosis,” due 31 October 2026 on the label Abanbandonment. Gare Terminus is the solo project of Margarita Omar.

“Kenosis” is a six-track album described as a collection of compositions influenced by noise, neofolk, drone, experimental and neoclassical music, combining intuitive arrangements and free improvisation with analogue and digital electronics. Its concept follows a mythological descent narrative, from self-emptying and threshold crossing through moral testing, revelation and abandonment to final judgment, mapped onto themes of war, mass culture, disillusionment and the search for meaning. The tracklist runs “Kenosis,” “River Styx,” “Benevolent Knife,” “Wisdom of the Forest,” “Abandoned Land” and “To the Death.”

About Gare Terminus

Gare Terminus is a Luxembourg-based neofolk, noise and experimental project led by Margarita Omar. The project released its first EP, “The Mass,” on 29 August 2024, a two-track release exploring themes of war, decay and mythology through martial industrial, noise and apocalyptic folk. “Kenosis,” out 31 October 2026 on Abanbandonment, is Gare Terminus’s first full-length album, previewed with the video for “Wisdom of the Forest.”

items.title: Orquídeas em Prosa releases ‘Beijo Nuclear’ single
items.summary: Brazilian harsh EBM/dark electro duo Orquídeas em Prosa released the single "Beijo Nuclear" on 16 October 2026, featuring guest vocalist Bárbara Tayná.
items.fullText:
Harsh EBM and dark electro duo Orquídeas em Prosa, from João Pessoa, Brazil, released the single “Beijo Nuclear” on 16 October 2026 on Bandcamp. The track features guest vocals from Bárbara “Barb Core” Tayná of Melancholic Wine and is the second of three releases the project plans before the end of the year.

Soturna Cröstä handles vocals, synths, drums and bass on “Beijo Nuclear,” with Tony credited for the lyrics. The track was recorded, mixed and mastered by Soturna Cröstä at Carmesim HomeStudio, with cover art by reptilian.creates. Describing the single’s theme, Orquídeas em Prosa stated: “In this single, we ambient a romance war aesthetic.” “Beijo Nuclear” is also available to stream on Spotify and YouTube.

The project’s third release of the year, “Queimante Sol,” is scheduled for 13 November 2026 and is currently previewing on Soundcloud ahead of its wider release.

About Orquídeas em Prosa

Orquídeas em Prosa is a harsh EBM and dark electro project from João Pessoa, Brazil, started by Soturna Cröstä. The project released its self-titled debut EP on 3 February 2026, a three-track collection recorded solo by Soturna Cröstä at Carmesim HomeStudio, followed by a second EP, “Ilegalismo Electro,” on 17 July 2026. Orquídeas em Prosa became a duo for the single “Lady Death,” released 18 September 2026, with Tony joining on lyrics. “Beijo Nuclear,” out 16 October 2026, is the duo’s second single and features guest vocals from Bárbara Tayná of Melancholic Wine. Orquídeas em Prosa describes its sound as exploring the dark side of technological progress through an anarchist, cyberpunk lens, alongside existential crises, warfare and revolution, and operates entirely DIY, self-producing its recordings and artwork. A third single, “Queimante Sol,” is scheduled for 13 November 2026.

items.title: Demokratie marks 5 years of ‘Perform & Consume’ with deluxe edition
items.summary: Munich duo Demokratie marks the 5th anniversary of "Perform & Consume" on 29 October 2026 with a 22-track deluxe edition featuring a new radio edit.
items.fullText:
Munich cinematic electronic duo Demokratie marks the fifth anniversary of its debut album, “Perform & Consume”, on 29 October 2026 with a 22-track deluxe edition. The expanded release compiles the band’s recordings since the album’s original 29 October 2021 release and closes with the first release of the radio edit of “The Wall Behind The Door.”

Thomaser and Knights first met in 2019 and released Demokratie’s debut single, “Ice Fall,” two years later. Thomaser also records as !distain, Arsine Tibé, The Grab Society and The Independent Seasons; Knights also records as KN/GHTS, Scarlet Soho and Boytronic. The original “Perform & Consume” came out as a six-track CD in a Lancing Pack gatefold sleeve, with the tracklist “Ice Fall,” “Speed Fight Date,” “Persistence,” “The Wall Behind The Door,” “Where Are You? (The Family Tree)” and “The Lookout (Seyhan III).”

About Demokratie

Demokratie is the Munich-based duo of Manfred Thomaser and James Knights, who met in 2019 and released their debut single, “Ice Fall,” in 2021. Thomaser also records as !distain, Arsine Tibé, The Grab Society and The Independent Seasons; Arsine Tibé has released several Side-Line-covered projects, including “The Lounge Noire Sessions” series. Knights also records as KN/GHTS, Scarlet Soho and Boytronic, and as Knights released the 2026 album “Supernatural Lover” on Specchio Uomo. Demokratie released “Perform & Consume” on 29 October 2021 and followed it with further material, including “The Lookout (Seyhan III),” “Speed Fight Date / Recession,” “(The Extended) Recession,” “Opaque” and the “Instrumental Imperative” series. The self-released 22-track deluxe edition of “Perform & Consume,” out 29 October 2026, closes out the first two chapters of the band’s discography with a radio edit of “The Wall Behind The Door” appearing for the first time, alongside instrumental versions of the album and singles and previously unreleased material including the “Public Debt I” demo and full-length versions of “Seyhan IV,” “Seyhan V,” “The Twilight Night” and “You Will Not Believe This.”

items.title: X & Stacy releases ‘Sangre Eterna’ single
items.summary: Chicago duo X & Stacy released the single "Sangre Eterna" on 19 October 2026, following their debut single "Love or Lust."
items.fullText:
Chicago body-beat duo X & Stacy released its second single, “Sangre Eterna”, on 19 October 2026. The track follows “Love or Lust,” the duo’s debut single released 2 September 2026.

Announcing the single, Jason Schmal detailed the band’s sound and influences: “We are a body beat duo from Chicago, Illinois that blends industrial, new beat, EBM, and synthpop together. We take influence from bands like Depeche Mode, Cetu Javu, Red Flag, Selena, and SPK,” he stated.

Yasmine Esparza handles vocals on “Sangre Eterna,” with Jason Schmal on synths and drum programming. Schmal also mixed and recorded the track, and John Scrip mastered it at Massive Mastering. “Sangre Eterna” is available as a digital track on Bandcamp.

About X & Stacy

X & Stacy is a body-beat duo based in Chicago, Illinois, blending industrial, new beat, EBM and synthpop. The duo released its debut single, “Love or Lust”, on 2 September 2026, followed by “Sangre Eterna” on 19 October 2026.

items.title: Midnight Zone – ‘Midnight Zone’ (Digital/Cassette Album – X-IMG)
items.summary: With Midnight Zone, we welcome a new American project founded in 2025 by Ian Hicks...
items.fullText:
With Midnight Zone, we welcome a new American project founded in 2025 by Ian Hicks and Mimi Chakravorty. Both have established backgrounds in the US scene and now combine their experience on their self-released debut, “Midnight Zone”, which features seven tracks.

From the very first seconds, you immediately recognize a fusion of Industrial and Techno, complemented by few female vocals. This approach continues throughout the album, occasionally enhanced with Acid sequences and, at other times, IDM elements. The overall sound is experimental, with both artists occasionally letting loose, yet it remains undeniably promising. While the combination of Dark-Techno and Industrial is hardly new, here it results in an effective blend with enough power to conquer dancefloors. Sparse vocals also make an appearance, delivered in a subtle, whispered style that genuinely adds an extra dimension to the music.

 Midnight Zone may not offer groundbreaking innovation, but this debut certainly left me wanting more. (Rating:7½).

Listen to:

https://midnightz0ne.bandcamp.com/album/midnight-zone

About Midnight Zone

Midnight Zone is an electronic duo from Los Angeles, California, formed in 2025 by Ian Hicks and Mimi Chakravorty. The project works with analog and digital sources and describes its sound as experimental techno and noise. Hicks and Chakravorty wrote and produced all seven tracks together.

The debut album “Midnight Zone” was released on X-IMG on 3 July 2026. Its tracklist runs “Intro”, “Psyops”, “Machine City”, “Bathyal Zone”, “Natural Selection”, “Tonic Immobility” and “Outro”. Hector Carlos Ramirez mastered the album at Factory Systems. This review covers the duo’s first release.

items.title: Chicago Duo X & Stacy Turn Vampiric Desire Into Body Beat Communion on “Sangre Eterna”
items.summary: Somewhere in the Windy City, a daring duo have apparently decided that the ideal soundtrack for eternal damnation should involve a drum machine, a considerable amount of sexual frustration, and… The post Chicago Duo X & Stacy Turn Vampiric Desire Into Body Bea
items.fullText:
Somewhere in the Windy City, a daring duo have apparently decided that the ideal soundtrack for eternal damnation should involve a drum machine, a considerable amount of sexual frustration, and the sort of theatrical excess that would make Dracula consider hiring a new stylist. X & Stacy, the body beat duo of Yasmine Esparza (X) and Jason Schmal (Stacy), have returned with their second single, Sangre Eterna, indulging their appetite for industrial electronics, Italo Disco, and European club music.

The proceedings begin with a funereal chime, that ancient announcement that somebody has either died or is about to make a spectacularly poor romantic decision. Eerie Spanish-language vocals drift into the arrangement, establishing an atmosphere of supernatural unease before a gloriously indecent backbeat barges into the funeral procession and starts rearranging the furniture. Suddenly, the cemetery has acquired a dance floor, and the mourners are behaving in ways that would get them excommunicated from most respectable religious institutions.

X & Stacy’s influences encompass the synthetic romanticism of Depeche Mode and Red Flag, the mechanical brutality of SPK, and the Latin pop sensibilities of Selena, an unlikely family gathering whose members would probably spend Christmas arguing over the thermostat. The song’s melodic sensibility also recalls the sleek synthpop of Cetu Javu, lending a seductive elegance to this peculiar congregation. Yet Sangre Eterna finds these ingredients getting along rather splendidly.

Minor-key synths conjure a mood of exquisite depravity as the rhythm section strides on with the resolve of a particularly horny undertaker. Through the electronics, a chamber-goth shimmer emerges: resonant, string-like tones that evoke hammered dulcimer or sitar. The passage summons the mystical grandeur of Dead Can Dance, lending the song an arcane, ritualistic air—as if the dance floor had been consecrated for a beautifully illicit ceremony.

The Spanish vocals are punctuated by gasps and moans that push the proceedings toward something deliciously absurd, suggesting an intimate encounter conducted in the basement of an abandoned nightclub. Then comes a screeching guitar passage that recalls the more unhinged experiments of Bauhaus, tearing across the electronic arrangement with the abrasive theatricality of Daniel Ash attacking a particularly troublesome piece of furniture. The collision of gothic rock and New Beat works beautifully, introducing a welcome dose of instrumental violence into an already wonderfully disordered affair.

One imagines this playing during a vampire film in which the bloodsuckers abandon their aristocratic obligations, raid a discount clothing store for leather trousers, and spend eternity getting thrown out of nightclubs. Frankly, immortality has seldom sounded quite so entertaining.

Listen to Sangre Eterna below and order the single here.

Having shared stages with Madeline Goldstein, Normal Bias, Choke Chain, and others, X & Stacy clearly know their way around the darker corners of contemporary club culture. Sangre Eterna suggests they’ve also developed a healthy appreciation for the pleasures of making drum machines behave badly.

Follow X & Stacy:

  • Spotify
  • Instagram

items.title: Gothminister – ‘We Are All Demons’ (CD/Vinyl Album – Elevator Records)
items.summary: Gothminister released its ninth studio album, "We Are All Demons," on 16 October 2026 via Elevator Records. Britta Pirkko reviews it for Side-Line.
items.fullText:
Norwegian gothic industrial metal band Gothminister, led by Bjørn Alexander Brem, released its ninth studio album, “We Are All Demons,” on 16 October 2026 through Elevator Records, on CD and vinyl as well as digitally. Brem recorded, produced, mixed and mastered the album himself. Britta Pirkko reviews “We Are All Demons” below.

Following the elaborate concepts of the two “Pandemonium” albums, Brem has chosen a more personal direction. This time, the demons aren’t supernatural creatures but the rather unpleasant things we all carry around with us. Fear, anger, insecurity, jealousy, painful memories. The sort of things that don’t disappear just because we would prefer not to think about them.

Interestingly, Brem recorded, produced, mixed and mastered the entire album himself. Considering how much is going on in Gothminister’s music, that’s quite an undertaking. And it has clearly given him the freedom to experiment with whatever musical ideas crossed his mind.

“Darkest Side Of Earth” opens with electronic textures before the heavier elements gradually take over. The title track, “We Are All Demons,” follows with a driving rhythm, a strong chorus and plenty of electronic energy. It’s catchy without sacrificing the darker atmosphere, and I wouldn’t be surprised to hear it regularly on gothic club nights.

“Nightmare King” brings the guitars further forward, while “The Dark” takes a more atmospheric approach. The contrast between Brem’s deep vocals and the female voice works particularly well here. There’s a certain vulnerability beneath the darker arrangement, which suits the song’s subject of separation and loss.

“The Spell,” featuring Thomas Jenssen, combines heavy guitars, electronic rhythms and melodic passages. “Welcome To Hell” is more straightforward, with an aggressive industrial metal sound and Brem’s characteristic vocals. I have always had a soft spot for that particular side of Gothminister. Heavy, direct and just theatrical enough to remind you who’s responsible.

And then there’s “Salsa.”

Yes, salsa. On a Gothminister album. I honestly don’t know why, but there’s something wonderfully amusing about this song. Perhaps it’s the unexpected Latin rhythms mixed with Gothminister’s familiar darkness, or simply the absurdity of the combination. Whatever it is, it makes me smile. And I rather like that.

“My Revenge” deserves special attention, particularly because of the story behind it. Brem has spoken about being bullied by someone he once considered a close friend. Years later, during a sold-out concert, he recognised that same person in the audience. This time, however, he was the one standing on stage, looking out at a crowd that had come to see him.

I find that story quite powerful. People who have experienced bullying know that the damage doesn’t necessarily disappear when the bullying stops. Sometimes those memories stay with you for years. The moment Brem describes isn’t really about getting revenge. It’s about realising that someone who once made you feel small no longer has any power over you.

Musically, “My Revenge” channels those emotions into a harder industrial arrangement, with aggressive electronics and a forceful vocal performance. Knowing the background makes the song particularly interesting to me. There’s a real person behind all that gothic theatricality, and sometimes it’s worth remembering that.

“Darkness Is My Throne” continues with heavier electronic elements, while “Fearless” brings a more melodic atmosphere and orchestral touches. The instrumental “There’s A Crown For All” closes the album on a grander note.

What I appreciate about “We Are All Demons” is that Brem hasn’t restricted himself to the usual Gothminister ingredients. Of course, the industrial guitars, dark electronics and dramatic vocals are still there, but he also makes room for dance rhythms, more melodic passages and some rather unexpected musical combinations.

Does everything fit together perfectly? Not necessarily. The changes between the heavier material and the more experimental tracks can be abrupt, and I can imagine that some listeners would prefer an album concentrating entirely on the industrial metal side of Gothminister. But I don’t mind the occasional detour. After so many years, I’d be much more disappointed if Brem had simply stopped trying new things.

What makes this album particularly interesting is the contrast between the familiar Gothminister image and the personal experiences behind some of the songs. The costumes, horror imagery and theatrical performances have always been part of the attraction, but this time there’s considerably more going on beneath the surface.

“We Are All Demons” isn’t necessarily the most consistent Gothminister album, but it has character, plenty of musical variety and some genuinely interesting ideas. I particularly appreciate that Brem is still curious enough to experiment, even when the results might divide his audience.

And I must admit, I never thought a Gothminister album would make me smile because of salsa.

‘We Are All Demons’ tracklist

“We Are All Demons” runs: “Darkest Side Of Earth,” “We Are All Demons,” “Nightmare King,” “The Dark,” “The Spell” (feat. Thomas Jenssen), “Welcome To Hell,” “Salsa,” “My Revenge,” “Darkness Is My Throne,” “Fearless” and “There’s A Crown For All.”

About Gothminister

Gothminister is the project of Norwegian musician Bjørn Alexander Brem, active for more than 25 years across eight previous full-length albums and performances in more than 40 countries, known for pairing gothic and industrial metal with horror imagery and theatrical live shows. In January 2024, Gothminister was a surprise candidate in Norway’s Eurovision Song Contest selection. The band shared the single “My Revenge” from the forthcoming album in July 2026, and announced “We Are All Demons” shortly after.

“We Are All Demons,” released 16 October 2026 via Elevator Records, is Gothminister’s ninth studio album and the first since the two-part “Pandemonium” series, moving from concept-driven material toward a more personal set of songs written, produced, mixed and mastered entirely by Brem himself.

items.title: Then Comes Silence announce new album ‘Requiem Ballroom’
items.summary: Then Comes Silence release "Requiem Ballroom," a new studio album, on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records, led by the single "Bye Bye Land."
items.fullText:
Swedish post-punk and gothic rock trio Then Comes Silence releases its seventh studio album, “Requiem Ballroom,” on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. The album is led by three singles already released since August: “Judgement Day,” “Remaker Redeemer” and “Bye Bye Land,” the last of which arrived on 16 October with its own music video.

“Requiem Ballroom” is built as a diptych: the first half, Requiem, represents darkness and farewell, while the second, Ballroom, moves toward light and renewal. Produced by frontman Alex Svenson, the album was recorded at two studios in Stockholm. The Requiem half was mixed by Tom van Heesch, whose credits include Rammstein, Backyard Babies and Apocalyptica, while the Ballroom half was mixed by Jon Bordon, known for his work with Nicole Sabouné, Melody Club and The Exploding Boy. Svante Forsbäck mastered the record at Chartmakers.
