Behind “Bye Bye Land” lies a personal story: Svenson has said the song was inspired by a close friend who went through life-changing trauma and reached a point of no longer wanting to be alive. He describes the song as a reminder of how much that person means to him and to those around him.

“Requiem Ballroom” follows “Trickery,” the band’s 2024 album, which the UK’s Classic Rock magazine praised for its “post-punk influence of Bauhaus or Joy Division offset by an ’80s windblown, cinematic sense of drama presented with silky production and confidence.” Vive Le Rock similarly described “Trickery” as a “huge, spectral sound that cascades the post-punk genres seamlessly.”

European and UK tour dates

Then Comes Silence supports “Requiem Ballroom” with mainland European concerts in early January 2027, plus a London date at The Garage in late May 2027.

About Then Comes Silence

Founded in Stockholm by vocalist/bassist Alex Svenson, Then Comes Silence has built its sound around horror, the occult and underground goth, post-punk and darkwave music. Early support from Germany’s post-punk scene turned the country into a second home for the band, backing years of touring across Europe. Following three independently released albums, the group signed to Nuclear Blast for “Blood” (2017), and has since shared stages with Fields Of The Nephilim, Clan of Xymox, The Chameleons and A Place To Bury Strangers, and played festivals including M’era Luna, Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Amphi Festival, Castle Party, Tomorrow’s Ghosts Festival and W-Festival.

Since 2022, Then Comes Silence has worked as a trio of Svenson, drummer Jonas Fransson and guitarist Hugo Zombie. The band released the “Boxed” EP ahead of 2025 European tour dates and toured Europe through summer 2024 behind “Trickery.” “Requiem Ballroom,” arriving 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records, is the band’s first full-length since that record.

items.title: Some Days Are Darker release single and video ‘NDRI’
items.summary: New York goth and synth trio Some Days Are Darker releases the single and official video "NDRI," taken from the forthcoming album "Black Box Warning."
items.fullText:
New York goth and synth trio Some Days Are Darker releases the single and official video “NDRI”. The track is also streaming on Spotify and Apple Music. “NDRI” is drawn from the band’s forthcoming album, “Black Box Warning,” recorded with Dave Catching at Rancho de la Luna in Joshua Tree, California.

Set against a driving electronic pulse, “NDRI” moves through the tension between emotional numbness and overwhelming sensation. “The things we desire in life are the same things that destroy us; that’s the beauty,” says Lear, the band’s frontman.

‘Black Box Warning’, recorded at Rancho de la Luna

“Black Box Warning” is a twelve-song album recorded with producer Dave Catching at Rancho de la Luna, the Joshua Tree studio also used by Iggy Pop, Queens of the Stone Age, Arctic Monkeys, Foo Fighters, PJ Harvey and Daniel Lanois. The record moves between some of the band’s most intense material and quieter, more exposed moments, including a solo acoustic performance and a closing piano ballad.

About Some Days Are Darker

Some Days Are Darker began as the solo songwriting project of former metalcore guitarist Lear Mason and has since grown into a three-piece with bassist/guitarist/keyboardist Chris Martin and drummer/multi-instrumentalist/producer Robbie Williamson. Based in New York, the band draws on the shadowy grandeur of goth, the hypnotic pulse of synth-driven alternative rock and the intimacy of noir cinema.

“NDRI” is the latest single from the band’s forthcoming album “Black Box Warning,” following its recording sessions with Dave Catching at Rancho de la Luna in Joshua Tree, California.

items.title: A Split-Second, Dirk Ivens and The Invincible Spirit to headline EBM night in Cologne
items.summary: A Split-Second, Dirk Ivens and The Invincible Spirit headline an EBM night at Club Volta, Cologne, on March 27, 2027. Tickets on sale now.
items.fullText:
Belgian EBM act A Split-Second, electronic music pioneer Dirk Ivens and German project The Invincible Spirit share the stage at Club Volta in Cologne, Germany, on Saturday, March 27, 2027. Each act performs a full-length headline set. Tickets are on sale now.

A Split-Second was founded in Belgium in 1985 by Marc Ickx and helped shape early EBM and the Belgian new beat movement, with tracks including “Flesh,” “Rigor Mortis,” “Firewalker” and “On Command.” The band’s Cologne appearance is billed as a best-of set covering its catalogue.

Dirk Ivens performs a set spanning four decades of his work with DIVE, The Klinik, Absolute Body Control and Blok 57, moving across projects rather than concentrating on one. He is joined onstage by Jan Dewulf of Mildreda, who also worked with Ivens on DIVE’s album “Where Do We Go From Here?”

The Invincible Spirit, the long-running project of German musician Thomas Lüdke, completes the bill. Founded in 1986, the project built its reputation on the debut single “Push!”, built around a bassline still played on EBM dancefloors.

Event details for the Cologne EBM night

The show takes place at Club Volta, Schanzenstrasse 6-20, 51063 Cologne, Germany. Doors open at 18:00, with the first set starting at 19:00. Tickets and event information are available now.

About A Split-Second, Dirk Ivens and The Invincible Spirit

A Split-Second was formed in Belgium in 1985 by Marc Ickx and became one of the acts associated with the birth of EBM and the Belgian new beat scene, releasing tracks such as “Flesh,” “Rigor Mortis,” “Firewalker” and “On Command” that remain in circulation among EBM audiences today.

Dirk Ivens has worked across several projects since the early 1980s, including DIVE, The Klinik, Absolute Body Control and Blok 57, and is regarded as one of Belgium’s pioneering figures in minimal electronic and industrial music. For the Cologne show he performs alongside Jan Dewulf of Mildreda, his collaborator on DIVE’s album “Where Do We Go From Here?”

The Invincible Spirit was founded in 1986 by German musician Thomas Lüdke and became a fixture of the EBM scene from its debut single, “Push!” The three acts’ joint appearance at Club Volta brings together close to four decades of EBM history in a single evening.

items.title: Puppenjunx announce debut album ‘Einz’, share single ‘Der Präsident ist tot’
items.summary: Puppenjunx, the EBM project of Orange Sector's Martin Bodewell and Lars Timm Felker, releases debut album "Einz" on 6 November 2026 via Infacted Recordings.
items.fullText:
German EBM project Puppenjunx releases its debut album, “Einz,” on 6 November 2026 through Infacted Recordings. The project is run by Orange Sector’s Martin Bodewell and Lars Timm Felker, who have already shared the first single, “Der Präsident ist tot,” digitally since 16 October, including an Orange Sector Club Mix.

Puppenjunx gives Bodewell and Felker an outlet for musical ideas that do not fit Orange Sector’s current direction, with a stripped-down, old-school approach to electronic body music. The project’s name references the historical German term “Puppenjungs,” associated with Hannover’s criminal history and the Fritz Haarmann case of the 1920s.

Limited CD edition of ‘Einz’

For the physical release, Bodewell and Felker have pressed a limited number of CDs, pre-orders for which are open directly through the band via Facebook Messenger.

About Puppenjunx

Puppenjunx is the EBM side project of Martin Bodewell and Lars Timm Felker, both also members of Orange Sector. Where Orange Sector has moved in its own direction over the years, Puppenjunx is built around a minimal, straightforward EBM sound closer to the genre’s old-school roots.

The project debuted its first single, “Der Präsident ist tot,” digitally on 16 October 2026, paired with an Orange Sector Club Mix. Its debut album, “Einz,” follows on 6 November 2026 through Infacted Recordings, with a limited CD pressing available directly from the band.

items.title: Lords of Acid release new album ‘Mundo Bizarro’
items.summary: Lords of Acid released "Mundo Bizarro" digitally on 15 October 2026, with LP and CD following 9 November via Metropolis Records, during their US tour.
items.fullText:
Belgian electronic dance act Lords of Acid released its new album, “Mundo Bizarro,” digitally on 15 October 2026, timed to the start of the second leg of the band’s “Cheeky Freaky” US tour. LP and CD editions follow on 9 November through Metropolis Records. The band had announced the album on 1 October, and it is the group’s first album of entirely new material since 2018.

The album collects the four singles Lords of Acid has released since April: “Karaoke Superstar,” featuring Princess Superstar; “Dream Boy,” featuring Carla Harvey; “El Mundo Está Loco,” featuring Tony & The Kiki; and “Ich Will Nur Das,” featuring Mari Kattman. Seven further new songs round out the eleven-track record.

“Karaoke Superstar,” “Dream Boy” and “Ich Will Nur Das” each arrived with their own official videos. Carla Harvey, formerly co-vocalist of Butcher Babies, joined Lords of Acid as the band’s “Acid Queen” in January 2025 and features on “Dream Boy.”

‘Mundo Bizarro’ tracklist

“Mundo Bizarro” runs: “Dream Boy,” “Dancing On The Flames,” “El Mundo Está Loco,” “Dopamine War,” “Maximo Roboto,” “Ich Will Nur Das,” “City Of Angels,” “So Stoned Today,” “Karaoke Superstar,” “You’re Obscene” and “A Viking’s Heart.”

Lords of Acid continues its “Cheeky Freaky” tour across the United States through 31 October.

About Lords of Acid

Formed in Antwerp, Belgium, in 1988, Lords of Acid became one of the most influential acts of the era’s hard-edged electronic dance scene, blending techno, acid house and industrial music with lyrics built around sexuality, drug use and hedonism. The band debuted with the New Beat single “I Sit On Acid,” and its 1991 debut album, “Lust,” was followed by a string of releases that made Lords of Acid a regular presence on the Billboard dance and alternative charts.

Carla Harvey, formerly co-vocalist of Butcher Babies, joined Lords of Acid as vocalist in January 2025, and the band toured extensively through the year, including the 2025 “Praise The Lords” tour. In February 2026, Lords of Acid announced the “Cheeky Freaky” US tour alongside work on new material, and in April 2026 the band shared the single “Karaoke Superstar” featuring Princess Superstar. “Mundo Bizarro,” out now digitally and on LP/CD from 9 November via Metropolis Records, is the album that single and its three follow-ups were building toward.

items.title: Pete Shelley’s ‘Sky Yen’ gets first-ever CD release via Cold Spring
items.summary: Cold Spring releases "Sky Yen," Pete Shelley's 1974 solo electronic recording, on CD for the first time on 27 November 2026, ahead of his Buzzcocks days.
items.fullText:
Cold Spring releases the first-ever CD edition of “Sky Yen,” the experimental electronic recording made by Pete Shelley in March 1974, two years before he co-founded Buzzcocks. The CD arrives 27 November 2026, in a matt-laminate digipak using Shelley’s original cover design with Malcolm Garrett.

Shelley made the recording while studying electronics in Bolton, before switching to philosophy and European literature, using an oscillator he built himself. Recorded on a two-track tape machine with added echo and effects, “Sky Yen” is built from electronic tones, drones, feedback and noise, shaped partly by physical contact with the oscillator’s circuitry.

Still a teenager at the time, Shelley had been listening to German electronic acts including Tangerine Dream, Cluster, Kraftwerk, Can and Faust, whose influence steered him toward a soundworld far removed from mid-1970s rock and pop. “Sky Yen” was eventually released by Shelley himself on his own Groovy Records label in April 1980, after Buzzcocks had already found international success, revealing how far back his interest in electronic experimentation went.

Shelley returned to that interest with the 1981 single “Homosapien,” written in 1974 as a Jets of Air song and co-produced with Martin Rushent. The accompanying album included several more songs written in the mid-1970s, and Rushent’s programming work on the sessions also fed into “Dare,” the album he was producing concurrently for The Human League.

‘Sky Yen’ tracklist and credits

“Sky Yen” is presented in two parts: “Sky Yen Part 1” (20:45) and “Sky Yen Part 2” (20:42), both performed by Pete Shelley on a purpose-built oscillator in March 1974. The CD layout for Cold Spring was done by Abby Helasdottir, reproducing Shelley and Garrett’s original cover design.

About Pete Shelley

Pete Shelley (1955-2018) was studying in Bolton and fronting the group Jets of Air when he recorded “Sky Yen” in March 1974. Two years later, he co-founded Buzzcocks, one of the acts that defined British punk and post-punk through concise, melodic songwriting.

Shelley self-released “Sky Yen” on his own Groovy Records label in April 1980, after Buzzcocks’ breakthrough, and followed it with the 1981 synth-pop single “Homosapien,” co-produced with Martin Rushent and originally written in 1974 as a Jets of Air song. Cold Spring’s CD edition, out 27 November 2026, is the first time “Sky Yen” has been issued on the format.

items.title: Suzi Sabotage interview: ‘I want to keep wandering into new stylistic territories’
items.summary: Suzi Sabotage discusses her single "Sacrifice," self-production, Finnish roots and Goths For Palestine in a Side-Line interview.
items.fullText:
Suzi Sabotage has always worked through contrasts. Her music can be stark and danceable, confrontational and vulnerable, rooted in contemporary electronics while reaching toward Finnish language, folklore and traditional instrumentation. Her new single “Sacrifice” sharpens those tensions further, examining what happens when trauma is redirected toward people who did not cause it and when pain begins reproducing itself through someone else.

In this conversation with Side-Line, Suzi speaks about the psychology behind “Sacrifice,” perfectionism and complete creative control, why Finnish changes the texture of her songwriting, the place of tradition in modern dark music, Goths For Palestine, international touring, and the need to keep moving beyond any fixed version of Suzi Sabotage.

Suzi Sabotage interview

Karo: “Sacrifice” is about trauma turning into sadism, specifically the way somebody who has been hurt can redirect that pain toward people who had nothing to do with the original wound. What interested you in that secondary movement of violence rather than the initial trauma itself? Is the song ultimately about pain, responsibility, or the moment when suffering stops being an explanation and becomes a choice?

Suzi: I’ve often explored the subject of first-hand trauma in the past, namely from the perspective of a survivor (e.g. “I Am The Storm”). This time around I wanted to write about trauma’s potential byproducts. Human nature is fascinating that way, how some seek to momentarily alleviate their pain by inflicting it on others. I wonder why it is that misery loves company and one would get such instant gratification from hurting somebody who did them no wrong, a phenomenon which is especially rife on social media. In this dynamic, the target often blames themselves and looks inward for signs that they deserved the abuse or simply weren’t worthy of being treated well, especially if they’re prone to suffering in silence. Ultimately, the song is about the target’s realization of the driving factors behind the actions of the abuser, something which can finally break the cycle.

Karo: The track alternates between a low, brooding vocal register and a lighter, more airy one. That contrast feels psychologically appropriate to the subject because cruelty and vulnerability are not always separate states. Were you consciously using different parts of your voice to represent different emotional positions within the same person?

Suzi: Yes, cruelty and vulnerability are certainly entwined here, like two sides of the same coin. While I often deliberately use this duality in vocal registers, this time around I actually didn’t do it consciously, at least to symbolize the states of cruelty and vulnerability. I originally envisioned the chorus to be belted as an expression of frustration, the idea of making it airy came later on. Still, it’s a beautifully poetic interpretation and now I wish it had occurred to me before – I love sound symbolism!

Karo: “Sacrifice” runs on a 130 BPM drum-machine pulse and draws on the vocabulary of 1980s electronic music, yet the lyrical subject is unusually heavy. Do you like creating that tension between a body that wants to move and a text that asks the listener to confront something uncomfortable? What can rhythm communicate about anger that words alone cannot?

Suzi: Most definitely, writing songs that contrast a danceable composition with thematically thought-provoking or even disturbing lyrics is what I love doing. For me, swimming in the deep, murky waters of human psyche is profuse with inspiration for lyrics. When the subject is complex and cannot be easily summarized in a few words (unlike it’s often with lyrics that are wholly positive or negative), when it’s charged with cognitive dissonance and conflicting emotions… that’s where it gets interesting. I do think that the tempo gives the message an assertive quality instead of just being a lyric about licking one’s wounds and indulging in victimhood. It’s more about getting that nasty feeling of being someone’s punching bag, in all its unfairness, out of your system, and then being able to move on, instead of remaining trapped in the loop of feeling sorry for yourself or worse, becoming yet another link in the chain reaction.

Karo: You wrote, mixed and mastered “Sacrifice” yourself. Complete control can be liberating, but it also removes the external person who might challenge a decision or tell you when something is finished. How has self-production changed the way you judge your own work? Are you more ruthless with yourself when there is nobody else in the room?

Suzi: I do have some trusted loved ones with whom I share my unfinished works to get an external insight, always asking them if some aspect of a given track could be improved. I’m really thankful for being able to do so, as this kind of feedback is indispensable. I’m certainly more ruthless and demanding with myself than before, painstakingly analyzing every single note and word in my songs. I’ve placed myself under much pressure to deliver tracks that stand out and I’m always wondering if something I do overly resembles something that has already been done, whether by myself or others, or if it’s just not riveting enough as a creation. That said, I do recognize how having that unhealthy habit often inhibits my creativity, making me overthink it instead of living in the moment and channeling whatever happens to ignite passion in me at the time. Lately, overthinking and perfectionism have been some of the most considerable challenges in my artistry, ones that I will have to overcome going forward.

Karo: Your solo catalogue has moved between English-language dark electronic material and Finnish-language work such as “Oodi Surulle” and “Suden synty”, including the use of the kantele. Does changing language alter the emotional distance between you and what you are writing? Is there material that becomes possible in Finnish that would feel false or diminished in English?

Suzi: Actually, English has been my dominant language for over a decade now, the one I use in the vast majority of my daily interactions. Even my inner monologue and notes to myself are in English, so I don’t find that it necessarily creates any emotional distance. Lyrics invariably “come to me” in a particular language and I wouldn’t dream of switching to another one in the process. Either way, they wouldn’t work in any other language without making considerable alterations. For instance, I wouldn’t sing a translated version of one of my Finnish songs, even in order to make it more understandable for a wider audience, because it would lose its spirit and potentially, some important devices as well, such as alliteration. After all, I began writing in Finnish again partly for stylistic reasons. When I had the idea to incorporate neofolk influences in my songs, I knew that Finnish is a perfect fit for that. I grew up with it and associate it with the imagery I use in those of my tracks that are most inspired by neofolk.

Karo: There is an interesting tension in your work between modern electronic production and elements connected to Finnish cultural tradition. When you bring an instrument such as the kantele into a contemporary dark context, how do you avoid treating tradition as aesthetic decoration? What makes an old cultural form feel alive rather than merely referenced?

Suzi: I love that you describe it as tension, as that’s precisely my intention with my music, for it to be charged with this kind of strangeness that is slightly jarring and captures the listener’s attention. I suppose that the unusual combination alone, darkwave and neofolk, makes the presence of tradition feel more genuine, or at least it’s not readily mistaken as some kind of a pantomime. These peculiar combinations are the essence of my brand of creativity. While at times I do enjoy being campy to have some lighthearted fun with my art, I usually balk at clichés and find no value in works that are unimaginatively trite. I don’t claim to be the most quintessential embodiment of Finnish traditions, but I’m ardently passionate about that aspect of my homeland, the ancient and the mystical, something that transcends eons and predates state and organized religion. When I engage in exploring these traditions, I feel a deep connection to them, in awe of the arcane realm before my mind’s eye. That is how I know that it’s not a mere ornament or reference as far as I’m concerned, but an intrinsic part of who I am and where I come from.

Karo: “Nazi Goths, Fuck Off” has clearly travelled beyond its original release, to the point that other artists covered it in 2025. When a song with such a direct political statement starts belonging to other voices as well, does its meaning change for you? Is there a point where a song stops being only your statement and becomes part of the language of a wider scene?

Suzi: The song does seem to have become an entity of its own, quite unexpectedly so. To say that I’m honored to have been covered by these living legends would be an understatement, and it makes the song even more meaningful to me. To this day, it’s still quite unbelievable, and it all happened within the span of one single year. By that time, I was already thinking that the song, originally released in 2021, has been long forgotten. The statement has always collectively belonged to other voices as well, after all I’m far from being the first antifascist in the scene. The marginalized people in our subculture, especially people of color, have been taking a stance against both overt and covert fascist ideologies in our scene since the very beginning. Both within the scene and in society at large, those ideologies pose the most immediate existential threat to the most marginalized of us, so their outspokenness about it has way more weight than mine. On my own end, I’ve always felt like I should put my privilege and platform to a good use and amplify the voices of those who came long before me, who have resiliently combated the harmful ideologies and made sure that today we have an existing subculture to begin with, whether they’ve been widely recognized for it or not. The credit for the statement belongs to them, even the credit for the fact that I hold these beliefs in the first place, as I’ve learned so much by listening to their perspectives. The statement certainly doesn’t belong to me alone, as I’m only one of the many fighting the good fight, using whatever resources at my disposal to make my personal contribution.

Karo: You also created Goths For Palestine, which has brought together a large number of artists around fundraising. Music scenes often describe themselves as communities, but solidarity becomes much more concrete when money, reputation and public positions are involved. What have those compilations taught you about the difference between a scene that shares an aesthetic and a scene that is actually capable of collective action?

Suzi: I originally migrated to the goth scene from the punk scene in the first half of the 2010s, so I bring an ample number of influences from there. Grassroots action and human rights are an integral part of the circles that I came from. While these practices in the scene have had their flaws and inconsistencies, political awareness was woven into the lyrics and oftentimes manifested in taking part in direct action against oppression through demonstrations, fundraiser gigs, and other grassroots initiatives, like boycotts. Fast forward in time to the early 2020s, when I’d been in the goth scene for a while already, I observed that Gen Z (who at the time were rather new to the goth scene given their younger age) were unabashedly vocal about the same ideologies that I hold. While I had already made some low-key initiatives within the scene, it was Gen Z who inspired me to cultivate it further. I find that the newer generations not only engage in the aesthetics of goth but are also unambiguous about their stance against inequality and genocide. And well, the compilations themselves have taught me that the potential of the goth scene to have that dimension of collective action was very real indeed. I don’t think that there exists a scene that can survive on a shared aesthetic alone, there must also be some deeper connection and ethos, one just has to understand it to harness it to a good cause. The general Zeitgeist of absolute individualism notwithstanding, in the vast majority of us there’s this profound need for engaging in collective action and solidarity.

Karo: Your history runs through post-punk with Masquerade, keyboards with Virgin In Veil, solo darkwave and synthpunk, Finnish-language neofolk-tinged material, and more recent collaborations. Do you still think of these as separate stylistic territories, or has the idea of genre become less useful to you as your own musical vocabulary has expanded? What tells you that something is recognisably “Suzi Sabotage” regardless of the instrumentation?

Suzi: That’s a good question, as there has naturally been some overlap. I’d say it’s the emphasis on modern influences that makes my solo project stand out from my previous body of work, a radical departure from drawing most of my inspiration from the classics. I’ve endeavored my current sound to be rooted in the present moment as well as looking ahead into the future. While in goth music there’s a fundamental reverence for the past and vintage soundscapes are recurrently revisited, it’s in many ways in constant evolution, much like every other genre. Personally, I’m all for it, embracing new artistic inspiration and ideas brought by, for instance, new generations of goths. I’d be quickly bored to tears if I let my sound grow stagnant by hyperfixating on bygone eras instead of exploring brand new and thrilling influences. I believe that it’s this curiosity and fluidity that defines my solo work.

Karo: You have toured in South America, the United States and across Europe, while your music also carries very specific cultural and linguistic roots. After playing to audiences in such different environments, have you noticed which parts of your work translate immediately and which depend much more strongly on cultural context? Has touring changed your understanding of what is genuinely universal in dark music and what only appears universal from inside the European scene?

Suzi: I view my international tours as kind of a cultural dialogue. While my music naturally carries elements of my own culture, I’m also there to learn about theirs. I greatly enjoy getting to know the locals and their language. Even when the audience doesn’t know or fully understand the lyrics due to a language barrier, the mood of the songs knows no such barriers and music as a universal language connects us. What’s more, the antifascist sentiment of tracks like “Nazi Goths, Fuck Off” has been readily understood and shared by audiences globally, and it’s the song that the audience members most often sing along at my shows and come to thank me for. Many have also been heartwarmingly curious about the kantele and Finnish language, even learning a few phrases by heart to say to me. I certainly didn’t expect to hear Finnish words spoken by the audience members in South America, but it’s always such a delightful surprise and means the world to me. Still, during my travels I must be above all mindful of the culture and customs of the country I’m playing in and be respectful of them. I’d never put my own culture first and demand that locals understand it or even show curiosity about it. After all, I’m a guest in their homeland and should always act with due respect. I think that with this approach we can both have a meaningful cultural interaction and an enriching, mutually enlightening experience. I’ve only played on three continents so far, four if you count my past projects, and even at that, it makes for a limited number of countries and amount of time to experience each scene, so I wouldn’t be able to assess them well enough to draw parallels or examine the differences. Each scene is special and unforgettable in its own unique way, but universal enough to be enjoyed by goths from any part of the world.

Karo: Looking ahead, are you more interested in expanding the world you have already built, or in disrupting it? What would feel more dangerous to you now: becoming too recognisable, or abandoning something that has become essential to your identity?

Suzi: I’d actually like to do both in equal measure, haha. I’m fond of what I’ve already created, and I love that it’s getting recognition, but as a natural shapeshifter, I want to keep wandering into new stylistic territories. Only time will tell how this will manifest, whether incorporating something new into what already exists or undergoing a cataclysmic transformation. It will largely depend on my mood, which is in constant fluctuation, so anything is possible, the only constant being the baseline of my values and alignment with the strange and unusual.

About Suzi Sabotage

Suzi Sabotage is the solo project of Helsinki-based Finnish singer, songwriter and producer Suzi Nyberg. Before beginning her solo work, she fronted the Helsinki post-punk band Masquerade and played keyboards in the deathrock band Virgin In Veil. Her solo catalogue began appearing in 2020, followed by the debut album “Postmodern Dystopia” in 2021; the CD edition was released through Wrocław label Bat-Cave Productions.

She signed with Berlin label Out Of Line Music in 2022. Her subsequent work has included “I Am The Storm,” Finnish-language releases including “Oodi Surulle” and “Suden synty,” “Love at First Bite,” and “She-Demon.” Her music has also incorporated the Finnish kantele alongside electronic production.

Sabotage is also the curator of the Goths For Palestine benefit compilations. The first volume appeared in November 2024 and the second in September 2025, with proceeds directed to humanitarian aid through ANERA.

Her latest single, “Sacrifice,” was released Oct. 15, 2026 through Out Of Line Music. Suzi wrote, mixed and mastered the track herself.

items.title: Corchorus releases debut album ‘Lost In Life’s Great Shadow’
items.summary: Dark folk project Corchorus releases its debut album "Lost In Life's Great Shadow" on Bandcamp, 16 October 2026, as a limited CD and digital download.
items.fullText:
Corchorus, a one-man dark folk project from the Pacific Northwest of the United States, released its debut album “Lost In Life’s Great Shadow” on 16 October 2026. The seven-track record is available as a limited-edition CD and digital download on Bandcamp, with mastering and distribution handled by Savo-Karelian Productions.

Corchorus performs under a burlap sack mask and describes the album as combining dark folk, goth rock and black ambient into what the artist calls an “atmospheric acoustic ritual.” The songs draw on desolate woodlands, decaying buildings and high strangeness for a folk-horror atmosphere. Corchorus wrote the material through stream-of-consciousness composition on themes of inner darkness, possession and melancholia.

Corchorus ties the writing process directly to the masked stage persona:

“The songs that I write come from some strange corner of my mind that doesn’t feel like myself. The music is a reflection of a smothered, faceless version of me, that’s why I chose to wear a burlap sack over my head,” Corchorus said. “I have a very ritualistic, ceremonial approach to performing songs. It really is like being possessed by the music…”

Opening track “Death Come Quickly” comes with an official music video produced by Savo-Karelian Productions.

Corchorus ‘Lost In Life’s Great Shadow’ tracklist

  1. Death Come Quickly (03:54)
  2. Words Asunder (04:35)
  3. Stone Chimes (02:58)
  4. Song and Scythe (02:58)
  5. Snakeroot Eyes (02:42)
  6. Lost In Life’s Great Shadow (07:46)
  7. The End In Ocean Foam (06:34)

Track two, “Words Asunder“, was released as Corchorus’s debut single on 2 September 2026, backed by a lyric video. The album was written and recorded during the first half of 2026.

About Corchorus

Corchorus is a one-man dark folk project originating from the Pacific Northwest of the United States. The artist performs with a burlap sack covering the face, a choice tied to the stream-of-consciousness writing behind the material, and describes the live approach as ritualistic and ceremonial. Zeraya contributed backing vocals and photography to “Words Asunder” and provided the photography for “Lost In Life’s Great Shadow.”

Corchorus introduced the project on 2 September 2026 with the single “Words Asunder” and an accompanying lyric video. “Lost In Life’s Great Shadow,” the project’s debut album, followed on 16 October 2026 on Bandcamp as a limited-edition CD and digital download, with mastering and distribution by Savo-Karelian Productions. The seven-track record carries “Words Asunder” over as its second song alongside six new recordings written and recorded during the first half of 2026.

items.title: Corvad releases ‘Flux Core’ and ‘Pyrocene’ on ‘Summer Eternal – Anthology Volume One’
items.summary: Corvad released "Flux Core" and "Pyrocene" on 14 October 2026 via "Summer Eternal - Anthology Volume One," written for the RPG "Red Rooster."
items.fullText:
Dark electronic and industrial producer Corvad released “Flux Core” and “Pyrocene” on 14 October 2026 through “Summer Eternal – Anthology Volume One,” a book-and-vinyl anthology from game studio Summer Eternal. Both tracks were written for “Red Rooster,” the studio’s forthcoming role-playing game. The vinyl edition pairs Corvad’s music with original tracks by Croatian artist Nemeček.

Red Rooster soundtrack on ‘Summer Eternal – Anthology Volume One’

Summer Eternal, a worker- and player-owned game studio collective, built the anthology around the public reveal of “Red Rooster,” a physics-driven RPG set in the fictional world of Arta-Tantor. The 500-page book pairs art, writing and game-design material with a 10-inch vinyl that carries two Corvad tracks and additional music by Nemeček.

The vinyl was limited to 3,000 copies and sold out at launch. Copies shipped to supporters worldwide. “Summer Eternal – Anthology Volume One” remains available as a digital album on Bandcamp, with Corvad’s two tracks listed as:

  1. Flux Core (3:22)
  2. Pyrocene (4:28)

About Corvad

Corvad is an electronic producer based in Herceg Novi, Montenegro. He released his debut album, “Prime,” on 4 May 2018. His second album, “Unreal,” followed on 12 November 2021 through his own label, Cosmism Records. The album’s track “Khomus” features vocals and khomus performance by Alisa Dolgunova, and its artwork was created by Seryozha Parshakov.

Corvad’s third album, “Rootless,” followed on 22 May 2025. He produced, mixed and mastered the album himself, with artwork by Polina Filatova. “Rootless” explores themes of immigration, displacement and the search for stability.

His production and remix work has been released through labels including Virgin Music, Universal, Mau5trap, Soma Records and Sony Music, and his music has appeared in “The Batman,” “The Penguin,” “The Equalizer,” “Heretic’s Fork” and the YSL Beauty campaign. “Flux Core” and “Pyrocene” are his first music written for a video game, released on “Summer Eternal – Anthology Volume One” alongside Nemeček.

items.title: Feyleux announce second album ‘Shadeweaver’, out November 6 on Swiss Dark Nights
items.summary: Feyleux releases the single "Remote Control" and announces its second album, "Shadeweaver," out November 6, 2026 via Swiss Dark Nights.
items.fullText:
North Carolina darkwave duo Feyleux announces its second full-length album, Shadeweaver, out November 6, 2026, via Swiss Dark Nights. The record is led by the single “Remote Control,” which opens the nine-track album.

Feyleux is Laurelei Ruroden, on vocals and synthesizers, and Erica Gilstrap, on guitar, synthesizers and programming. The duo wrote “Shadeweaver” mainly over the winter of 2025 and 2026, blending gothic rock and dreampop with 1980s new wave textures, airy vocals and cold guitars. The band builds the record around dark romanticism and Jungian shadow work, confronting the suppressed or rejected parts of the self.

“Shadeweaver” follows “Remote Control” with “Frailty,” “Grave Moss,” “Flutter + Fade,” “Detachment,” “Oubliette,” “Solitary World,” “Astral Weaver” and “Strawberry Moon.” The album is available to pre-order digitally and on CD in a digipak limited to 500 copies through the label’s Bandcamp.

Feyleux’s chronology since ‘Midnight Hearts’

Side-Line first covered Feyleux with its debut album, “Midnight Hearts,” released June 7, 2024, via Swiss Dark Nights, following a demo EP from January 2024. The nine-track debut was mixed and mastered by Kurs (Valerio Rivieccio) and opened with “The Empress,” whose music video arrived June 6, 2024. Feyleux returned in February 2026 with the three-track EP “Phases,” featuring “Frailty,” “Mercury” and “Shoreless.” “Shadeweaver” is the duo’s follow-up, due less than three years after its debut.

About Feyleux

Feyleux formed in North Carolina in mid-2023 as a duo built around Laurelei Ruroden and Erica Gilstrap, blending dreampop and darkwave electronics with a current of 1980s synthpop. The band released a demo EP in January 2024, followed by its debut album, “Midnight Hearts,” on June 7, 2024, via Swiss Dark Nights, mixed and mastered by Kurs (Valerio Rivieccio) and led by the single “The Empress.” The duo has played more than a hundred shows since that debut and returned in September 2025 with the video for “Phantoma,” followed by the three-track EP “Phases” in February 2026. “Shadeweaver,” the band’s second full-length, arrives November 6, 2026, again via Swiss Dark Nights, carrying the dark-romanticism and shadow-work themes of its lead single, “Remote Control.”

items.title: Priest release ‘Dehumanized’, final single before ‘Altered State Police’
items.summary: Priest releases "Dehumanized," the third single and video from "Altered State Police," out October 23, 2026 via Blue Nine.
items.fullText:
Swedish dark synth act Priest releases Dehumanized, the third and final single from its fifth studio album, “Altered State Police,” on October 16, 2026. The album itself arrives October 23 via Blue Nine.

“Dehumanized” is track eight of the twelve-song album. It follows “Python,” released August 21, and “Minions,” the album’s second preview single. An official video accompanies the track, directed by Claudio Marino for Artax Film and starring Karo Hall, shot in a fetishistic, cybernetic style. The video follows a character whose survival instincts strengthen after being stripped down in the aftermath of a relationship.

Priest dedicates the song to “all survivors out there” and to victims of people with narcissistic personality disorders. The band says the song and video do not romanticize trauma. Their stated focus is the emotional cost of realizing what has been lost and the struggle to reclaim one’s identity.

‘Altered State Police’ tracklist and production

Altered State Police runs: “Jaded” (feat. Internal), “Python,” “Jeopardize,” “Altered State Police,” “Karmageddon,” “Sentimental,” “When We’re Gone,” “Dehumanized,” “Minions,” “The Savior’s Blade,” “Here Comes the Light” and “Stargate” (feat. Unify Separate). Linton Rubino and Leo Josefsson produced the album; Josefsson mixed it at Kiss the Needle, and Magnus Lindberg mastered it at Redmount Studios. The record moves through surveillance, technology, identity and political distrust, mixing synthpop, industrial electronics and 1990s big beat.

“Altered State Police” is available to pre-order on CD, black 180g vinyl, and a red 180g vinyl pressing limited to 300 copies, with a red sleeve variant limited to 150 copies.

Priest tours Europe and the UK from October 24 to November 28, with stops in Sheffield, Whitby, London, Paris, Köln, Berlin, Oberhausen, Munich, Frankfurt, Hannover, Leipzig, Hamburg and Stockholm.

About Priest

Priest is a masked Stockholm act formed by former members of Ghost, blending 1980s sci-fi aesthetics with gothic soundscapes across synthpop, industrial and electronic textures. The band released its first single in 2017 and has since built an international following among synth, EBM and industrial listeners, with releases including “New Flesh,” “Body Machine” and “Cyberhead.” Priest has also built a parallel catalogue of covers, including Rammstein’s “Engel” in 2023 and, the same year, Depeche Mode’s “Personal Jesus”, released by a lineup including former members of Ghost.

Side-Line first covered “Altered State Police” when Priest shared the single “Python” in August 2026, following the band’s US tour supporting Stabbing Westward. “Minions” followed as the album’s second single. “Dehumanized” now closes out the album’s single rollout ahead of its October 23 release on Blue Nine, after which Priest heads into a European and UK tour running through late November.

items.title: Souls In Bondage – Souls In Bondage (Digital/Cassette EP – Sister9 Recordings)
items.summary: Souls In Bondage is a Dutch-Italian duo making their debut with this self-titled EP, presenting...
items.fullText:
Souls In Bondage is a Dutch-Italian duo making their debut with this self-titled EP, presenting five tracks of what they describe as Noise-Rock.

I detect 1980s influences that evoke the grey area between Dark-Wave and Cold-Wave. While the specific label isn’t crucial, it does offer a clue to the sound: Souls In Bondage create dark music featuring both male and female vocals—although, to my ears, the female voice has a slightly more enchanting quality. The guitar plays a prominent role, yet the addition of synths lends extra power to the overall atmosphere. The duo seems to be striving for a unique sound, unafraid to incorporate experimental passages or even a track with hints of Shoegaze.

I wouldn’t call this an extraordinary debut, but it is certainly a promising record from a group that is still finding its footing while already showcasing some cool ideas. (Rating:6½).

Listen to “Mild At Heart”:

About Souls In Bondage

Souls In Bondage is a post-punk and noise rock duo formed in the autumn of 2025 by Simona Dellamorte and Giulio Pardi, who are based between the Netherlands and Italy. Dellamorte, also known for Feralia Planitia and Atrate, plays synths and shares vocals, while Pardi, also of Bibo & Beyond, contributes guitar alongside a drum machine.

The duo released their self-titled debut EP on Sister 9 Recordings on March 6, 2026, as a digital download and a limited-edition cassette, with five tracks: “Orbiter,” “Fallen,” “Island Universes,” “Blank,” and “Mild at Heart.” Sister 9 Recordings previously released Nothingheads’ debut album “The Art Of Sod” in February 2025.

items.title: Dread Risks release ‘Hellhymn Remixes’ EP via Re:Mission Entertainment
items.summary: Dread Risks released 'Hellhymn Remixes', a 3-track EP reworked by Antigen Shift, Frontal Boundary and The Proximity Assembly, out 16 October 2026.
items.fullText:
Austin, Texas electro-industrial duo Dread Risks released “Hellhymn Remixes” on 16 October 2026 through Re:Mission Entertainment. The digital EP gathers three new versions of the band’s 2025 single “hellhymn,” reworked by Antigen Shift, Frontal Boundary and The Proximity Assembly.

The release runs just under 14 minutes across three tracks. “hellhymn (Antigen Shift Hellfire Burn Remix)” opens the EP at 4:41, mixed by Antigen Shift and mastered by Dread Risks. Frontal Boundary handled the second remix, “hellhymn (Frontal Boundary Remix),” at 4:01, mixed and mastered with Brendin Ross. The Proximity Assembly closes the EP with “hellhymn (The Proximity Assembly Remix)” at 4:52, which the act also mixed and mastered.

Re:Mission Entertainment described the EP as a release that “continues the 2026 momentum created by popular singles ‘where you left’ and ‘invertebrate.'” The original “hellhymn” single came out on 1 August 2025 on the same label.

“Hellhymn Remixes” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp.

About Dread Risks

Dread Risks is an industrial duo from Austin, Texas, signed to Re:Mission Entertainment. Side-Line first covered the band in August 2021 with the video premiere for “Trauma Ties,” followed two months later by the premiere of “Obliteration Complex.” In March 2022, the duo released the album “Automated Disappointment” on Re:Mission Entertainment, premiered on Side-Line the day before its release.

Remix collaborations followed through 2023: a God Module remix of “Machine Identity” in March, a pairing with French industrial duo Moaan Exis on a remix of “Comadose” in July, and a video premiere for “Extinction Form” in September. The band released the single “hellhymn” on 1 August 2025 through Re:Mission Entertainment.

Dread Risks opened 2026 with two further singles on the label, “Where You Left” in March and “Invertebrate” in April, before returning to “hellhymn” for the three-track remix EP released in October.

items.title: Octolab – Words From A Stranger
items.summary: Upbeat, energetic and mystical: Octolab are back with “Words From A Stranger”. A synth pop treat well worth a listen.
items.fullText:
Octolab’s epic return

Octolab are finally back and, with “Words From A Stranger” from their latest album “Waiting For A Better Ending”, present a won­der­fully upbeat and ener­get­ic track. The band builds a son­ic ten­sion that seems on the verge of burst­ing, car­ried by majest­ic, epic choruses.

Octolab them­selves clas­si­fy the track as future pop. To be hon­est, I’m not sure wheth­er I can fully con­firm or refute that. The rap­id BPM and the rous­ing energy cer­tainly sup­port it and make this assess­ment entirely under­stand­able. Sonically speak­ing, how­ever, the track strikes me more as a form of mys­tic­al synth pop with a fas­cin­at­ing Enigma-esque touch. For me, this song is def­in­itely well worth a listen and won­der­fully refreshing!

Listen to "Octolab – Words From A Stranger" on Spotify

items.title: Spectres Of Desire – Entanglement
items.summary: Rich analogue synths and honest vocals. Spectres Of Desire surprise with the mature synth pop track ‘Entanglement’.
items.fullText:
How Spectres Of Desire transform emotional pain into captivating synth pop

Rich ana­logue synths, a crisp beat and nos­tal­gic melod­ies, this is exactly how synth pop should sound that sticks in your head straight away. When you then real­ise that this artist is new to the genre and is politely ask­ing for feed­back, you’re left truly amazed. ‘Entanglement’ sounds aston­ish­ingly mature, as if the American solo artist had been breath­ing in dark synth pop sounds since childhood.

I was par­tic­u­larly impressed by the vocals. They come across as pleas­antly hon­est and largely do without any mask­ing effects. This lends the track a won­der­fully raw, authen­t­ic qual­ity. Lyrically, you can sense this depth in every line. The song tackles the heavy theme of intergen­er­a­tion­al pain and the desire for redemp­tion with a sombre, poet­ic pull. An abso­lutely mature piece of work that leaves you want­ing more.

Listen to "Spectres Of Desire – Entanglement" on Spotify

Listen to "Spectres Of Desire – Entanglement" on Bandcamp

Lyrics of "Spectres Of Desire – Entanglement"

I've been walk­ing, col­lect­ing causeways
across dream­s­capes of wasted life
A par­al­lel tale, her own per­son­al hell
being with him till the day he died

I've been des­per­ate, weakened and reckless
a salt mine on a quiet rail
She's seen glimpses, reflec­ted moments
of shad­ows call­ing us bey­ond the veil

Some day, he'll be, just anoth­er man who for­got his life
Some day, she'll see, that there's just no way to get out alive

He fell off men­tally, shock­ingly quickly,
a child's mind is a curse to bear
She sloughed off slowly, not even knowing,
a soft shield before her organs failed

She soaked in com­fort, wrapped up in loathing
in lock-step with a raging squall
I dove in quickly, hastened the drowning
seek­ing echoes of that shad­ows call

Some day, I'll see, there's anoth­er way to get out alive
Some day, you'll be, bliss­fully aware of anoth­er life

items.title: Erk Aicrag interview: ‘Curiosity interests me much more than purity’
items.summary: Erk Aicrag (Hocico, Rabia Sorda) talks to Side-Line about Pingo, MANIC, Chuntata Boys and leaving Mexico for Germany.
items.fullText:
For more than three decades, Erk Aicrag has been immediately recognizable as the voice and physical force of Hocico, but his creative life has long since expanded beyond a single project or medium. Alongside Rabia Sorda, he writes books and poetry, performs spoken word, creates soundtracks, works with Eric13 in Chuntata Boys, developed the dance-theatre piece “The Sound of Bodies Breaking” with Giulia Mandelli, and is now building MANIC with Patrick Heaney. Rather than treating these projects as separate identities, Aicrag increasingly sees them as different places in which the same creative impulse can take form.

In this conversation with Side-Line, he speaks about recognising when aggression becomes formula, why reading poetry to 40 silent people can feel more exposing than performing for thousands, how leaving Mexico changed his understanding of his own cultural identity, and why uncertainty has become more valuable with age. He also discusses Rabia Sorda, “Unseen Horror Scenes,” Chuntata Boys, MANIC and a creative philosophy increasingly driven by curiosity rather than the need to defend a fixed idea of who he is.

Erk Aicrag interview

Karo: You currently work through Hocico, Rabia Sorda, your books and spoken word, your own soundtracks, and Chuntata Boys. When an idea appears, do you already know which language it belongs to, or does the form itself reveal what the idea really is?

Erk Aicrag: These days I normally let the idea tell me where it wants to go.

I don’t sit down and say, “Okay, today I have to write something for Hocico, Rabia Sorda, Chuntata Boys…” or “this should become a poem.” Sometimes it starts with one sentence, sometimes with a sound, sometimes just with a feeling that bothers me and I don’t even understand yet why.

I get these little Eureka moments all the time, so I write almost every day. Over the years I’ve built this strange personal database of phrases, fragments, images and ideas. Some of them sit there for years doing absolutely nothing. Then suddenly I’m working on a song, a poem or something else and one of those old fragments speaks to me again. It has found its place.

Having different projects gives me a lot of freedom in that sense. I don’t have to force every part of myself into one. Some things need electronics and screaming. Some need guitars and drums. Some become stronger when there is almost nothing around them except my voice and the words. Sometimes even the voice is too much and it really is only the words.

And now I have MANIC, a new project with my friend Patrick Heaney. That has opened another door. We’re working toward our first single, “Into The Static,” and it already has its own personality. I really enjoy that feeling of entering a new room without completely knowing what is inside yet.

Maybe that’s what I appreciate most at this point as a creator: I have different places where ideas can live. I don’t expect one project to carry everything that is inside me.

Karo: “Unseen Horror Scenes” looks at paranoia, addiction and forms of social decay connected to contemporary digital life. Early Hocico drew much of its aggression from very tangible surroundings and lived experience. Has your anger become less geographical over the years and more concerned with systems and human behaviour itself?

Erk Aicrag: Definitely. When Hocico started, a lot of the anger came directly from what was around us. Mexico City was everywhere in the music: violence, inequality, pollution, corruption, chaos, that constant pressure around you. And of course we were very young, so you absorb all of that in a very direct way. There wasn’t much distance between what was happening outside and what came out of us.

Now I’ve lived in Germany for more than twenty years and travelled through many places of the world, and you start noticing that many things you thought belonged to one particular place are actually everywhere. The scenery changes, but people are still dealing with fear, loneliness, addiction, manipulation, frustration, the need to belong.

Digital life has made that even more visible to me. And I’m not anti-technology at all, quite the opposite, I love technology. What fascinates and worries me is what we do with it and what it does back to us. We have never been so connected technically, yet there is an incredible amount of isolation. We voluntarily carry devices that demand our attention every few seconds and then wonder why we cannot concentrate, why we compare ourselves constantly or why we feel anxious.

So yes, the anger became less geographical. I’m probably more interested now in systems, but also in human behaviour itself: what is being done to us, but also what we willingly do to ourselves.

The horror isn’t always somewhere outside anymore. Quite often we’re carrying it around in our pockets.

Karo: After more than thirty years, aggression is no longer simply an instinct in Hocico; it is also something you know how to construct extremely well. How do you recognise the difference between anger that is still artistically necessary and aggression that has merely become part of a familiar vocabulary?

Erk Aicrag: That is something I think about quite a lot, because aggression can very easily become a costume or even a brand in a band like Hocico.

After more than thirty years, of course we know how to do certain things. Racso knows how to build tension in a track, I know what I can do with my voice, and we both know what people will immediately recognise as Hocico.

And exactly because you know those tools so well, you have to be careful. Craft can very easily become formula.

If I scream simply because “Hocico screams,” I’m not really interested. I’ve done that already. There has to be something underneath it that I genuinely feel.

What has changed for me is that I don’t automatically associate intensity with volume anymore. When I was younger, if I was angry, I wanted to destroy everything with it. Now I know that sometimes one carefully chosen sentence can be much more violent than somebody screaming in your face.

Of course I still love the aggressive side of Hocico and Rabia Sorda. Otherwise I wouldn’t still be doing this. It is part of the DNA of those projects and probably part of mine too.

But aggression needs a reason. Otherwise it becomes decoration.

Karo: Rabia Sorda gives you guitars, drums, Punk and a much more visibly physical band dynamic, while Hocico remains rooted in electronic construction with Racso. Do those projects allow you to express different sides of the same personality, or have they gradually produced genuinely different versions of you as a performer?

Erk Aicrag: A little bit of both. They definitely started as different sides of the same person, but after so many years I think each project has also taught me a different way of being on stage.

Hocico has something almost ritualistic for me now. The moment certain sounds begin, my body knows that world immediately. There is a tension and a darkness there that has been developing for more than thirty years. I don’t really have to think about becoming that person anymore. It just happens.

Rabia Sorda feels completely different physically. Having Marco behind me on drums, Titus with the guitar and sometimes Giulia on percussion changes the way I move and react. A drummer hitting behind you pushes your body differently from a programmed beat coming through the monitors. There is more punk energy, more dirt, more of that feeling that something could go slightly (or very) wrong. I love that.

And now with MANIC I’m discovering another version again. The interesting thing is that Patrick and I don’t have thirty years of history telling us what this project is supposed to be. We are still finding out. I had almost forgotten how exciting that uncertainty can be.

But I don’t see any of them as characters I put on. They’re all me.

Maybe it is the same nervous system using different muscles.

Karo: “No Hay Dolor!” brought Rabia Sorda back with new recorded material after a relatively long interval. At this point, what does Rabia Sorda give you creatively that Hocico still cannot: not stylistically, but psychologically?

Erk Aicrag: Freedom from history, in a way. Hocico is something I’m extremely proud of. It changed my life completely. But when something has existed for more than thirty years, there is inevitably history attached to everything new you do.

There are expectations from the audience, of course, but there are also expectations inside yourself. You’re always having a conversation with everything you did before, whether you want to or not.

Rabia Sorda has always felt lighter to me psychologically. It still connects very directly with that childish dream I had of being in a rock’n’roll band. A loud band in a room, drums behind you, guitars, sweat, mistakes, energy.

I can be more impulsive there. More punk. More rock’n’roll. Sometimes even a little stupid in the best possible way. I don’t have to analyse everything. If something feels exciting, sometimes that’s enough.

I think that becomes very valuable when you’ve been making music for such a long time. You need places where instinct can still beat experience occasionally.

I want to keep surprising myself. Hopefully other people too.

Karo: I saw you at NCN on the Lesebühne with “Words Like Razors,” where there was nowhere for language to hide behind volume, distortion or a large production. Has reading your work aloud changed the way you write lyrics, because you now hear immediately whether words can stand without music supporting them?

Erk Aicrag: Absolutely. And honestly, standing on a small stage with only a microphone can be more frightening for me than standing in front of thousands of people with Hocico or Rabia Sorda. At the reading at NCN I am sure you felt that.

With those projects there is volume, lights, distortion, adrenaline, movement. There are so many things happening at the same time. On a reading stage, if the sentence is bad, there it is. Naked. Everybody can hear it, and most importantly, I can hear it.

That has definitely changed the way I look at words.

I don’t think every lyric has to work as poetry without music. A song has its own language. Rhythm, repetition, pronunciation, even the physical sound of a word can be part of what makes a lyric work.

But reading aloud has made me much more sensitive to bullshit in my own writing.

Sometimes I write something and it looks fantastic on the page or on the screen. Then I say it aloud and think, “Come on, man, what the fuck is this?” You suddenly hear somebody trying very hard to sound profound.

Delete. That’s a very useful filter.

Karo: “Pingo” deliberately combines poetry, narrative, visual material and your soundtrack “The Noise Is Unavoidable.” When the same emotional world can exist as text, image and sound, do you still think in terms of separate works, or are you increasingly interested in building one larger artistic environment through different media?

Erk Aicrag: I’m definitely becoming more interested in the larger environment.

With Pingo I really felt that happening. The writing created images in my head. Then the images suggested sounds. Sometimes the soundtrack changed the way I understood something I had written months before.

None of those things were simply illustrating the others. They started having a conversation with each other.

That opened something for me.

When I was younger, I thought much more in categories: this is an album, this is a book, this is a concert. Today those borders are much less important to me.

If an idea wants to become text, music, movement, photography (or all of those things) why should I stop it because somebody needs to know which shelf to put it on?

We recently pushed that idea further with “The Sound of Bodies Breaking,” the dance-theatre work I developed with Giulia Mandelli. It became a very intense project for us, something we poured a lot of energy into over a long period of time. There you have bodies, spoken language, sound, atmosphere and movement all influencing each other. I find that incredibly exciting, because suddenly music is not only something you hear; it changes the way you perceive a body moving through a space. We definitely want to take the piece to other stages in the future and continue developing it.

I still love making songs. I will probably always love making songs.

But I also like the idea that a work doesn’t necessarily have to end when the song ends or when you reach the last page. If the idea still has somewhere else to go, I want to follow it.

Karo: Writing prose or poetry also allows ambiguity to remain unresolved in a way that the physical directness of Hocico often does not. Has becoming more serious about literature given you permission to leave certain questions unanswered instead of converting them immediately into confrontation?

Erk Aicrag: Totally. And I think age has a lot to do with that too.

When you are young, certainty feels incredibly powerful. Something is wrong, somebody is the enemy, you know exactly where you stand and you want to scream it. There is something beautiful about that energy and I don’t regret it.

But then you live longer and things become more complicated.

People you love die. People you trust disappoint you. Somebody you dislike can suddenly surprise you in a positive way. You realize you’ve contradicted yourself a thousand times. You make decisions you once swore you would never make. And eventually you also understand that the person telling the story isn’t always completely reliable, including yourself.

Literature gives me a place where I don’t have to solve all of that.

I can put two contradictory feelings beside each other and allow both of them to be true. I can write about something without immediately deciding who was right and who was wrong. Sometimes I can simply say, “I don’t understand what happened here.”

Years ago that uncertainty probably would have frustrated me. Now I find it fascinating.

I still love confrontation. That hasn’t disappeared. But I don’t believe anymore that every sentence needs to end with an exclamation mark.

On the page I don’t have to win the argument. That feels like freedom.

Karo: With Eric13 and Chuntata Boys you deliberately use the term “Lizard Music” for something that refuses a conventional genre passport. After spending most of your career inside scenes with very strong identities and codes, how liberating, or perhaps how difficult, is it to make something whose first task is not to belong anywhere?

Erk Aicrag: It is incredibly liberating. And I say that with enormous affection for the scene I come from. The industrial and gothic scene gave us a home at a time when we really needed one. Hocico became part of that culture in a way Racso and I could never have imagined when we were making tapes in Mexico City. Later Rabia Sorda followed its own path through that world too.

I will always be grateful for that.

But every scene develops rules, even scenes created by people who hate rules. That’s one of the funny things about subcultures: eventually even rebellion develops a dress code.

After some years you know which sounds belong, how people are supposed to look, what is considered authentic and even what kind of rebellion is acceptable.

So “Lizard Music” with Chuntata Boys is partly Eric13 and me having fun with all of that. It is our way of saying: don’t ask us what box this belongs in because we don’t know and, honestly, we don’t care.

If tomorrow we want electronics, guitars, mariachi, noise, something ridiculous or something that really shouldn’t work together, that’s probably exactly why we should try it.

At this point curiosity interests me much more than purity.

Karo: You left Mexico City for Germany in 2005 and have now spent more than two decades living there. I wonder whether distance changes artistic belonging in unexpected ways: has living abroad made you more conscious of what in your work is genuinely Mexican, and what you once assumed was cultural but was actually simply personal?

Erk Aicrag: Absolutely. When you live inside your own culture, you don’t recognise half of it because it is simply normal to you.

I think I understood how Mexican I am much more clearly after leaving Mexico. Funny enough, I even started embracing Mexican music much more while living in Germany. Things I hadn’t necessarily paid much attention to when I was surrounded by them suddenly spoke to me differently from a distance.

And it goes much deeper than music or the obvious cultural symbols.

The relationship with death. The way tragedy and humour can exist in the same sentence. Family. Religion, even if you’re not religious like me. Violence. Superstition. The ability to laugh in the middle of a terrible situation. That strange combination of beauty and brutality that can feel completely natural when you grow up with it.

At the same time, Germany changed me enormously. I’ve spent a huge part of my adult life there. My family is there. My routines are there. Some of the way I think now is German too, whether I notice it or not.

So I don’t feel any need to decide, “Am I Mexican or am I German?”

I’m very Mexican. I’ve also been profoundly shaped by Germany. And there is some strange third country inside me that exists only because I’ve lived between the two.

Sometimes you have to leave the picture before you can really see its colours.

Karo: You move between extremely exposed forms of expression: screaming in front of thousands of people, reading something personal in a small room, writing alone, producing sound in private. Which of those situations now makes you feel most vulnerable, and has that changed as you have become more experienced?

Erk Aicrag: The small room, for sure. Put me in front of ten thousand people and there is actually a strange kind of protection in it. A huge crowd can almost become one organism. There is noise, adrenaline, darkness, lights and more than thirty years of physical memory telling me what to do. Things can still go wrong, of course, but I know that territory extremely well.

Now put me two metres away from forty people sitting quietly while I read something personal that I wrote alone at three in the morning…

That’s different.

Those are forty individual faces looking back at you and silence is brutal.

Writing alone is vulnerable too, but nobody sees all the terrible versions before something becomes good. Nobody watches you deleting the paragraph you thought was genius the night before.

When you read something aloud, there is nowhere to hide.

The funny thing is that experience has made me much more confident as a performer, but it has also made me deliberately interested in situations where I’m not completely confident.

And I don’t want to spend the rest of my creative life only doing things I already know I can do.

Feeling vulnerable means there is still something at stake and I need that.

Karo: Looking at everything you are doing now, I get the impression that “Erk Aicrag” has become broader than the role of frontman, even though Hocico remains central. When you look ahead, are you interested in expanding that artistic territory even further, or is the next challenge to make these different strands speak to one another more deeply?

Erk Aicrag: Both, probably. But more and more I’m interested in understanding how all these things belong together.

For most of my life as an artist, people understandably knew me first as the singer of Hocico. And I’m incredibly grateful for that. Hocico changed my life.

Because of this band I travelled around the world, met people I would never have met otherwise, stood on stages I never imagined I would stand on and built a large part of my life around creativity. And after more than thirty years, I can finally look back with enough distance to understand that this music actually meant something to people.

Believe me, that is a strange and beautiful thing to realize.

When you’re inside the storm, inside of your music career, you’re always thinking about the next album, the next tour, the next problem, the next train or flight. You don’t really stop and think, “Wow, this thing we made somehow became part of somebody else’s life.”

I appreciate that much more now. I don’t take it for granted.

But I also understand that being the frontman of Hocico is one part of who I am and not the complete definition.

I love writing. I love making soundtracks. I love spoken word. I love Rabia Sorda. I love doing something completely strange with Chuntata Boys. I loved developing “The Sound of Bodies Breaking.” And now MANIC with Patrick gives me that beautiful feeling of starting again. Our first single, “Into The Static,” is coming soon, and I’m excited about building something without already knowing what the finished world is supposed to look like.

I don’t see any of those things as distractions from each other anymore. They’re different outlets for the same person.

And maybe that is one of the interesting things about getting older creatively. When you’re young, you’re desperately trying to define who you are. Then you spend years protecting or defending that identity. Eventually, if you’re lucky like me, you realize you don’t have to defend it anymore. You can just keep moving.

I don’t feel the need to prove that I can do many different things. I’m much more interested in finding the connections between them and following those connections wherever they take me.

After all these years, curiosity is still probably the most important thing I have. If I ever lose that, then I should probably stop.

About Erk Aicrag

Erk Aicrag is a Mexico City-born vocalist, songwriter, producer and writer best known as the frontman of Hocico and founder of Rabia Sorda. He began making music with his cousin Racso Agroyam in 1993, when Hocico took its definitive form; the duo released its first album, “Odio Bajo el Alma,” in 1997. Aicrag later created Rabia Sorda in 2003 as a separate outlet for material that could move beyond Hocico’s established framework. He relocated to Germany in 2005 and has lived there since.

His work has increasingly extended beyond conventional album formats. Aicrag has presented his writing publicly through “Until My Throat Bleeds / Words Like Razors,” a collection incorporating poetry, short prose, reflections and previously unpublished lyrics. In January 2026 he followed it with the illustrated book “Pingo / The Damage Is Unavoidable,” combining poetry, narrative and visual material; its accompanying 20-track soundtrack, “The Noise Is Unavoidable,” was composed and produced by Aicrag and released in late 2025.

Across these projects, his work now encompasses electronic music, punk- and rock-oriented performance, poetry, spoken word and soundtrack composition, alongside the continuing activity of Hocico and Rabia Sorda. Side-Line previously covered Hocico’s 2026 album “Unseen Horror Scenes.”

items.title: Lex & Hood release synth-pop single ‘Automate Automate’
items.summary: Bicoastal duo Lex & Hood releases the satirical synth-pop single "Automate Automate" on Flipside Records, out October 15, 2026.
items.fullText:
Bicoastal duo Lex & Hood released the single “Automate Automate” on Flipside Records on October 15, 2026. The track is a satirical synth-pop and new wave song with a darkwave sheen, built around a deadpan female lead vocal and running 3 minutes 26 seconds at 129 BPM, aimed as a send-up of the AI boom.

Lex & Hood is the songwriting partnership of Lex Ventura, based in Santa Barbara, California, and Tom Hood, based in Tampa Bay, Florida. The two previously worked together as Lex & The Hood before reuniting in 2026 to release a run of new songs on Flipside Records, including “Face of America,” “Annoying,” “Rats in a Cage,” “Shut Up and Listen” and “The Light Outside My Window.”

“Every Lex & Hood song is written by Lex and Tom: the lyrics, the melodies, the concept. We use AI-assisted tools for parts of the production and some video imagery, so the finished track sounds the way we hear it in our heads,” the duo states on its website.

“Automate Automate” is available to stream on Spotify.

About Lex & Hood

Lex & Hood pairs Lex Ventura, who draws on classic pop-rock, R&B, synth and surf influences, with Tom Hood, a performing singer-songwriter who mixes blues, rock, country and island-flavored styles. The two previously recorded together as Lex & The Hood before reuniting in 2026 and signing to Flipside Records, where “Automate Automate,” released October 15, 2026, follows earlier singles including “History Repeats Itself” and “Rats in a Cage.” The duo credits AI-assisted tools for parts of its production and video imagery, while writing all lyrics, melodies and concepts themselves.

items.title: Ekospell releases synthpop single ‘Creatures Of The Night’
items.summary: Athens synthpop duo Ekospell released the single "Creatures Of The Night" on September 25, 2026, with an official video out via Ekospell Music.
items.fullText:
Ekospell, an electro/synthpop duo from Athens, Greece, released the single “Creatures Of The Night” on September 25, 2026, through Ekospell Music. The band posted an official video for the track on YouTube on October 17, 2026.

The track runs 5 minutes and 35 seconds and follows “Automated,” a single Ekospell issued in 2023. Vocals are credited on the band’s Instagram to @martzitrikka, with @spirosanalog handling analog synthesizers and production. The band describes its sound as built around analog equipment, synthesizers and drum machines, aiming for what it calls a “pure 80’s sound.”

“Creatures Of The Night” is available to stream on Spotify.

About Ekospell

Ekospell is an electro/synthpop duo based in Athens, Greece, pairing analog synthesizers and drum machines with vocals. The band released its debut single, “Automated,” in 2023, followed by “Creatures Of The Night” on September 25, 2026, with an accompanying video issued on October 17, 2026.

items.title: La Nuit Américaine – La Voix Des Incendies
items.summary: La Nuit Américaine win you over with light electro pop: Why ‘La Voix Des Incendies’ has me hooked despite my initial doubts.
items.fullText:
A captivating slow-burner with youthful naivety

To be hon­est, it’s quite rare for me to fea­ture a track on Electrozombies where I’m not 100% sure at first glance wheth­er it fits the bill per­fectly. That’s exactly how I felt at first about “La Voix Des Incendies” by the French duo La Nuit Américaine.

The track is more of a slow-burn­er: light elec­tro pop that son­ic­ally leans notice­ably towards Chromatics. At first I wasn’t all that con­vinced, but the track pos­sessed an unob­trus­ive magic and simply wouldn’t let me go. Ultimately, the song com­pletely cap­tiv­ated me with its very own, youth­ful naiv­ety. A fas­cin­at­ing listen­ing exper­i­ence that keeps get­ting better.
